I didn't get in on this game until a few years after it had already been out, but since then it has been nothing if not worth it. Play it in VR, or on your desktop or laptop, play it any way you want, it will run, and if you even have just slightly better specs than the minimum you will have a glorious time. The free updates have kept me periodically coming back, and now I want nothing more that to play this again at least once a month. Seriously, this game is nothing like what I heard people describing it 10 years ago. The devs have fixed, then added to, then gone above and beyond for this game, for this labor of love. If you can't afford the full price, I get it, and just wait for it to go on sale, but if you can, absolutely pay full price, as you will get your money's worth and so much more.

Likes: Over 18 quintillion different planets to visit, so there's always something new somewhere. The ability to discover and rename plants, animals, minerals, planets, and star systems. Incredibly immersive. Quite good writing on both main and side quests. There's such a diversity of things to do - tired of exploring? gather resources instead. Sick of that? do some base building. Dislikes: The freighter build systems sucks. It's insanely frustrating, with no real tutorial or guidance. The galaxy map has icons that aren't always intuitive. Speaking of which, merely hovering your cursor over a star system causes the game to consider that a "visited" star system, clogging and confusing your visited systems list. TL:DR. Immersive, diverse, and overall lots of fun with a few minor hiccups.

I love you, No Man's Sky. from the start, to the end of the 16th minute. Here's to another 10 years of an amazing game. On the 10th anniversary of this game, I realized that I never actually scored or wrote a review for what has always been one of my most wanted and favorite games—despite perhaps not having as many hours in it as in some others. Today, 10 years later, I am waiting for the release of Light No Fire to lose myself in their next world, which I feel is even closer to what I love in games. This team worked so hard and managed to reach a "Very Positive" rating on Steam after years of steady climbing and giving us amazing update after update. Just read the latest interview articles where Sean mentions that reaching an "Overwhelmingly Positive" rating is almost a mathematical impossibility. Well, here's to you, Sean. To the whole team at Hello Games, and to No Man's Sky. To your fans, you are already there.

There are many puzzles to figure out to open up new aspects of the game. Some aspects seem lame though. Spending time cooking meat gathered from dead animals is dumb for a video game. A demonstration of procedural technology. From my perspective, fundamentally boring. My opinion is more mixed. Yes, the game has some good vibes and can be enjoyable as an experience, but it’s not nearly as wholesome as you might expect it to be. Maybe I’m simply too experienced as a player, or perhaps I’ve spent too long working in game development, but all the variety I saw here amounted to multiple combinations of just a handful of visual and gameplay elements. Discoveries don’t excite or surprise you the way they do, for example, in Outer Wilds - instead, they mostly leave you bored. The repetitive combat and tedious resource grinding do little to help you immerse yourself in the adventure. I constantly feel like I’m restricted in what I can actually do as a player. Recommended for those who have plenty of free time and accept the idea of the journey being its only reward.

I love this game. I like many games, so don't think it is my favorite. But I really, really like it. It IS a survival game, because you have to collect and manage certain resources to load multiple systems. O2 for your survival, anti-cold, anti-heat, anti-toxic and so on are in the beginning the same, but you can upgrade your protection against certain types. So you can have different equipment for different planets. If you want. You have to manage charges for your mining equipment, for your weapons, for your spaceship's shield, for the spaceship's thrusters, for the spaceships jump drive and so on. And there are often better and more effective types of charge which you have to buy or manufacture yourself. But there is no hunger or thirst. Which at first is stupid, because there is food. But after a while you - or at least ME - will start to appreciate it. It makes it so, that you will have to plan for survival when you are on your way, because being in a storm and not being able to recharge your personal shield you will have to die. But when you are in a safe place you have all the time of the world, which is so relaxing. You can read the log and knowledge entries in the system without having to fear you die of hunger. You are in a safe place and can just stand there and read or plan or think or google or build a base or whatever you want. NO STRESS! That is good. I love it. I like for example Empyrion - Galactic Survival, but having to eat every 5 minutes or you are going to loose health is just not funny after a while. I think both systems have their place and No Man's Sky showed me that this system is very good if you want to play a survival game and still relax from time to time. Currently I can just mine in the ground and create a cave if the storm is too brutal and continue my voyage on foot after the storm is gone. No stress. :-) There are "normal" spaceships which you will mostly use. They are specialized. At least I think they all are. There are fighters and cargo ships. Probably more but these I remember. You can upgrade the ship's base per se and you can add equipment and get better equipment. Better drives, weapons, shields, whatever. There are a lot of planets and you can - kind of - move freely between them. Lots of resources. You can create so many bases, you will probably never get to the limit. I read it somewhere around 600 bases or so. You can add teleporters to your bases, so you can collect materials from the bases which have mining machines. You can grow plants or collect stuff. You can create stuff. You can buy and sell stuff. You can get rich just being a trader between systems, if you want. Never even tried it. I just love to collect resources. Later you can get a larger ship which can have up to nine of the original type landed, if you own so many. Even later you can buy frigates and send them on missions. They will come back - hopefully - and give you all the resources they collected. The universe is large and looks incredible good. The game mechanics are easy to understand and work perfectly. This is what you call an AAA game for a reason. I just love this game. What I love too: Battletech, Cities:Skylines, Crime Boss Rockay City, Dust to the End, Empyrion, House Flipper, Titanfall 2, Elite Dangerous (WITH Odyssey), Skyrim, Jagged Alliance - Back in Action, Carrier Command: Gaea Mission (not the FPS parts), and many, many more :-)

No Man's Sky will be played for 10 more years at minimum, and maybe even 100. I won't lie. The game has flaws, and bugs, and the occasional graphic issue. It's not perfect - but it is a masterpiece. Yes, there are 18 quintillion planets, and many are the same. But the procedural generation is actually superb. The game has enough oddities and unique points of interest to be interesting for a very long time. The game's main progression is linear but everything else is not. You can do countless things. Build a base on a planet - or on a freighter. Fish, fight, tame, explore. No Man's Sky has all the generic hallmarks of a basic survival game, but all mechanics are fleshed out and unique. No Man's Sky also has the paradox of being a single player MMO. Without use of the anomaly or (player built) city worlds, you may never meet another soul. Not to say you can't play with a select few individuals. I will put in a warning for those who think this is a spaceship combat game - it's not. No Man's Sky is truly one of the greatest games.
10 years still playing, 40 free DLC - just buy it!

No Man's Sky is probably one of the biggest gaming comebacks ever. The best part of the game is the feeling of freedom. You can find a planet, land basically anywhere, build a base, explore for a while and then get back in your ship and fly straight into space. Even after hours of playing, finding a genuinely beautiful or completely weird planet never really gets old. There's also way more to do than I expected. Building bases, upgrading ships, finding better gear, fighting pirates, managing a freighter or just exploring systems can easily turn "I'll play for an hour" into an entire evening. It isn't perfect. Planets can start feeling similar after you've seen enough of them, some of the grinding gets repetitive, and sometimes you spend more time managing your inventory than actually exploring space. But considering where this game started and what it has become, it's honestly impressive. No Man's Sky is the kind of game where you can have absolutely no plan, pick a random star on the galaxy map and somehow end up on an adventure. 8.5/10

Its a game that promised the moon (well, quadrillions of moons) and has spent 10 years shooting past that moon into the stars with free update after free update. You start out on an alien planet with no memory of how you got there and a basic signpost; you learn how to document your journey, collect some resources, and head out into space. Its not a tremendously deep game; you wont be making crazy, universe-altering decisions, or developing romantic relationships with NPCs, or stopping some BBEG from erasing existence (at least, not yet; who knows what the next updates will bring?). You're going to fly from planet to planet, start system to star system, seeing a few variations that after a few hundred hours may blur together. But if you're lucky, before you hit that point, you'll find friends and a community that has been around for a decade welcoming newcomers. If you're lucky, they'll share with you the magic they found in accepting the game for what it is, andallowing their dreams for what it could be to remain in dreamland. You'll see folks hosting days long dance parties, distributing hundreds of millions of credits worth of goods for free, or fishing for hours on end, chatting with each other before happing through a portal to the other end of the galaxy, never to be seen or heard from again. If you're lucky, you'll find folks who make sure you find the magic in the mundane, and help you to love splashing around in that "puddle" for years to come. See you in the cosmos, friend! PS the hours logged only represent my steam copy; my ps4 copy had many, many more hours logged.

No Man's Sky is an extremely fun exploration and survival game that allows explore, discover, fight, and build in an almost infinite and beautiful procedurally generated universe. You can use a massive variety of single person ships or larger multiplayer ships called corvettes that you can make from the ground up using dozens of unique ship parts (for the most part only the corvettes you can completely customize thought there are some smaller ship types that you can make and color by selecting cockpit, wings, engine, and reactor), or massive freighter capital ships to explore the universe with. On foot traversal includes a variety of vehicles ranging from large six wheelers and mechs, to small hover craft that let you glide over almost any terrain easily and large motorbike like things, or you can do it the old fashion way and just walk. The combat, at least on foot, isn't too much to talk about gameplay wise which deterred me slightly before I first got it but I decided to give it a try and it has become one of if not my favorite game ever.

10 years later and the devs are still updating the game free of charge and for the love of the fans. They could have sold out and pumped it full of microtransactions and paid DLC but instead they took a PR disaster and turned it into a most beloved game.
There is no greater redemption story in Video Games than No Man's Sky. Thank you, Hello Games, for your historic dedication.

There are times you stop and cant help but just stare at the beauty of a sunrise on an alien planet. Other times you hide in a hole from brutal fire storms sweeping its surface. Sometimes you work your way through alien infested derelict freighters looking for salvage. Sometimes you spend the day collecting and battling creatures. Maybe you'll just sit on your ship's wing as it bobs in the water fishing off the side and just enjoying the vibes. And best of all, the entire game can also be played in VR. There truly is nothing like No Mans Sky; and after 10 years of playing I still cant get enough.

I don't often leave reviews. I've been wanting to play this game for years but lacked the rig to run it. I first purchased it a few years ago on sale, finally started playing recently, and I have fallen completely in love with it. I'm a big fan of open-world sandbox games where I can experience things at my own pace. The exploration across different planets and systems is amazing—many locations are literal works of art. The flora and animals can look so wild that it’s mesmerizing. I especially love the water effects when building right on the surface and underwater. There are so many ways to build and be creative. It feels like a mix of an FPS, Animal Crossing, space combat, and even fishing if that's your thing. I was never one to play multiplayer, but this game made it fun. The cross-platform play makes it even better because I'm not stuck in a single ecosystem. I racked up 200+ hours in my first month, and I ended up purchasing an Xbox specifically to play this one game—and to play with friends and family who aren't usually gamers (my mom and little sister included), who ended up loving it too. Six weeks in, I'm at 350+ hours across two systems. I wouldn't blindly recommend it to everyone since everyone's tastes differ, but I'm very glad I bought it on Steam and ended up purchasing a second copy on Xbox to support the developers. They made a great game that, even 10 years later, looks AAA and runs wonderfully across Steam, Xbox, PlayStation, and Switch 2. It’s amazing playing with my family, friends, and new people I've met across platforms—plus, cross-save makes switching seamless. It is definitely a keeper, and something I’ll be playing for the next decade even if multiplayer ever fades out. I just realized how long this review is, so I'll sign off here. Like I said, I'm not someone who usually leaves reviews, but this game definitely deserved it. P.S. I can see myself getting a PlayStation 5 Pro down the line just to try out VR mode! 🫡 P.P.S. The complete lack of microtransactions is a massive win that locked me in for good.

This game is a unique gem and Im glad I tried it out. I am simply too invested in another space sandbox game with resource mining and cant really be invested in multiple games of this trope. That being said, I love all the nuanced ways this game is unlike any other game Ive ever played. I had absolutely no idea what to do at first and was frustrated, but I watched enough YT vids that it gave me hope that eventually Id "get to the good part" (2026 - if you research the game's history, this makes a lot of sense). The uniqueness of this game is great in all the right ways. Given the overall state of gaming in the 2020s, this is a must try, even if youre not into the genre. Just flow along with the tutorial and use a web search when you get stuck (if you do). The graphics are nice, I played with full everything on the steam deck and it was a really fun and relaxing experience. The visuals and color in this game are incredible. Being able to just point a spaceship and fly from wherever youre at to whatever youre looking at is really fun. Simply digging tunnels and "researching" weird flora and fauna is relaxing and fun. I cant explain it, this game doesnt exactly have any kind of goal, yet there is so much to do you cant express it well unless you play it a lot. I saw this company is doing an MMO using this engine, so Id probably want to play that given how cool this game was.

[h2]TLDR:[/h2] My favorite space game. [h3]Long Version:[/h3] We all know about the amazing comeback story of this game. Honestly, it is very impressive where the game is now. As for the actual gameplay, I love it. I really enjoy that there is such a variety of things to do in this game. The expeditions are very fun and offer cool rewards. Settlements offer something that I can check on occasionally when I don't have time to play the game much that day. The standard space station missions for the mercenary guilds are a nice way to pass the time and earn modules when starting out. It is also cool that I must actually learn the various languages the aliens speak to properly understand them. The corvettes are my personal favorite part. It is amazing seeing the awesome designs the other players can make. I'm slowly gathering parts for my own corvette, but it will take some time. I can't really think of anything I don't really enjoy in this game. If I am being nitpicky, I guess it would be nice to have more social experiences in the game and for the expeditions to be catalogued for players who missed them previously. Overall though, this game is wonderful, and I highly recommend picking it up. Also, for those who don't wish to buy the game at full price, I've noticed that NMS goes on sale nearly every month. Stay safe travelers!

In short, I recommend this game. In long, be aware of the limits of this game. The game has rightly been criticized and lauded for its expansive nature. Ten years after release, it still astounds. And yet the infinite randomness comes to feel like a series of stopwatches preventing the player from their actual desired gameplay. Resources are precisely far away from each other, different outposts are precisely difficult to find, different markets are exactly impossible to game. Like any game, No Man's Sky is fun within the limits set by the gameplay loop. For a game of infinite possibility, it is the sameness that eventually becomes glaring. I recommend this game, but I also recommend not playing it for too long or too often. Also the main story is flimsy, and because of the bite-sized nature of it, every plot point carries the same amount of weight. Whether you're meeting a new character, or realizing that someone is condemned to endless suffering, every plot point gets ten sentences, a search, resource collection, and then an abrupt ending. The language learning feature is one of the coolest features I've ever seen in a game. It's worth playing for that feature alone.

Cant recommend this game for $60 and is a hard sell at $30. I'm 20 hours in and everything I've found so far has just been largely disappointing, with nothing sticking out. Questing is so boring since its just running between places doing brainless tasks and because of that I'm just detached from the story. Nothing really feels polished either and the lack of settings is really annoying, I hate having toggle sprint when you can't infinitely sprint but I cant turn it off. I also ran into weird really bad performance issues that forced me to restart my game to get rid of it, which sucks because that means I am forcefully warped to my friend since I join off of him. Honestly the breaking point for me was the mech, it would've been so easy to make it really useful and cool and a big step up in progression but instead its just lame. Its probably useful if you invest a bunch into it but why do I have to unlock it via a quest, then have a bunch of research then go grab a bunch of items, some expensive some annoying, and then install it just to not have it be a walking storage unit. And if I want to have it follow me automatically I have to do another questline or spend more on research and materials, but even then I have to bring a teleport pad with me where-ever I go since I cant load it onto my corvette. Then multiplayer just doesn't work, like it literally breaks everything. Even if you're just in the same galaxy you can end up not being able to complete quests or even board your freighter. There is also no real reason to do multiplayer since there's no real cooperative play. The most cooperative play that I found so far was just doing corvette missions since your progress combines towards the same goal. The core of the game feels alright but everything around it is just such a pain to deal with, and considering the amount of bugs in multiplayer it just cannot be marketed as a coop experience. I honestly feel like the most fun path would be ignoring the intended gameplay path and just causing carnage, which other games can do better for less money. A bit all over the place, but basically: 1. Multiplayer doesn't work even after a decade 2. Questing is boring 3. Gameplay generally feels lackluster (This point is probably preference)

The biggest issue is that many of the main missions feel like extended tutorials rather than meaningful story progression. A lot of my time was spent traveling back and forth between planets, stations, and NPCs instead of experiencing exciting gameplay. The constant travel eventually became repetitive. The final Atlas mission was especially disappointing. After completing such an important objective, having my ship and multitool completely damaged felt more like a punishment than a reward. Instead of feeling satisfied after finishing a major storyline, I was given another repair grind. That completely killed the sense of achievement for me. I understand this may fit the game's design philosophy, where the journey never truly ends, but players who enjoy games with clear progression and rewarding conclusions may find this frustrating. What I loved: Beautiful universe and atmosphere. Excellent base-building system. Great freedom to explore. Amazing visual updates over the years. What I didn't enjoy: Main missions often feel like long tutorials. Too much repetitive travel between objectives. Story progression feels slow. The ending of the Atlas path doesn't feel rewarding. Damaging the player's equipment after a major milestone discourages rather than motivates. Overall, I respect the incredible work and dedication the developers have put into No Man's Sky over the years. It's simply not the type of progression-focused experience I personally enjoy. I may return in the future if friends want to play together, but as a solo player, I was hoping for a more satisfying sense of accomplishment after completing the main storyline.

I remember years ago when this game initially released a review along the lines of "Wide as an ocean, deep as a puddle". So I stayed away. I at some point but this game back on my wishlist since the overall sentiment online appears to be praise for the devs for supporting the game and making it much better and more fleshed out. Even the steam page is still 91% positive at time of writing. Finally decided to pick it up. I genuinely cannot fathom how shallow the game used to be if this is the better version, because that review I half remember from years ago is still 100% true. The game is so vast, but so very shallow. I've got over 80 hours entirely in the last 2 weeks. The core of waking up on a planet get a ship to explore and survive is cool. I want to find out why I'm here and the game explicitly makes you question what you are and why you are doing anything. Not a unique idea but the way it's presented is quite entertaining... until you start to see how little game there actually is here. To call it survival crafting is a misnomer, because at default settings you are at 0 risk of death in 99% of circumstances. In 80 hours I died once and that was from attacking a group of giant mechs with a mining laser then standing there getting shot trying to switch to my gun. It's a crafting game with survival mechanics that mean nothing. And damn does this game LOVE crafting. So much of your time in the game is resource collecting and inventory management. And it has the cardinal sin of [b]NOT BEING ABLE TO CRAFT [i]IN YOUR INVENTORY WITH MATS FROM STORAGE 10 FEET AWAY[/i]. HOW DOES EVERY GAME KEEP ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ THAT UP.[/b] *ahem* There is also a space-trucker trading economy hiding in the extremely boring cookie cutter space stations. Base building. Make money, buy personal ships, buy capital ships, build a fleet, customize to your hearts content. That's not a bad thing, in fact it's the best part of the experience. But the game wants you to think there is a reason, a WHY. And there just isn't. For all your ability to customize and build up your base and your ships and your fleet, you have 0 ability to affect anything in the universe other than your own little fiefdom. The story "quests" are presented like you have a choice, but you don't. Every quest is find a thing with the radar on your ship and go there. Maybe get a sting of text that describes something cool that may or may not be happening like a text only adventure game from the early 80's. Think ZORK except it's only 1 prompt and it's being played in an overlay while a massive 3d universe sits in the background crying. The prompts in these text dumps make it seem like you have a choice, but if you choose anything but the 1 choice that moves the quest forward the game tells you (literally in more than once instance) that you absolutely must do it only one way. You can do it in a ship you built from scraps and customized to your needs which you then land in your massive cool ass base, but there is no purpose at all beyond just doing it. This all sounds very negative but I didn't play 80 hours by accident. I certainly don't regret buying this game for $35. The base building and customizing your ship is satisfying if tedious due to [b]A GLARING OVERSIGHT FOR A GAME THAT IS 50% CRAFTING STUFF.[/b] The feeling of getting in your ship flying off a planet, landing on a different one and exploring is extremely fun, even just flying your ship like a plane on the same planet makes everything feel big. The space combat is even really fun once you turn off all the terrible console control defaults. The basic "get in ship and go" gameplay feels very smooth and is a very good hook to keep you wanting to be a part of the universe. Overall the game gives you all the dopamine spiking beeps and boops that make you feel good about accomplishing tasks. However, that very familiar dopamine mining formula is where the game completely falls apart for me. The only reason I kept launching the game was I felt addicted to coming back to manage my bases and settlements, to my capital ship and fleet of random bird frogs I hired to do missions while I'm offline. But they cannot affect the universe in any way. Once i saw it I couldn't unsee it. The "improvements" the game made are just the old MMO/mobile game addiction strategy to keep you playing. It is admirable the game does not have microtransactions to capitalize on this... but really why bother. Every planet in the universe is the same boring procedurally generated nothing with a different skin until you do a mission or just go far enough that another cookie cutter event/building/trading post gets generated. There is nothing unique about any planet or any station or any NPC. It's the same reskinned everything everywhere until you get bored and play something else. Wide as an ocean, deep as a puddle.

I’ve Held My Tongue Long Enough: A Candid Critique from a Devoted Fan I want to start by saying that this is one of the best games I have ever played, and I dont think I'll ever truly hate it. This game has come an incredibly long way since its launch, and everyone who has worked to build it into what it is today should absolutely be proud of what they've accomplished. However, after hundreds of hours of playing, there are several things that have become increasingly difficult for me to overlook. Some of these issues are minor annoyances, while others feel like major oversights that actively work against what the game is trying to accomplish. So, I've held my tongue long enough. NPC starships in space feel intentionally coded to annoy you simply for playing the game. Youll try to mine resources from asteroids, and an NPC will intentionally glide right in front of your crosshairs every five seconds the entire time you're mining. Even if you fly to a new area, the NPC will appear again and continue disrupting your mining. Youre essentially punished for simply playing the game. I don't care whether this is a bug or an intentional game mechanic tied to the deep lore of the game. This type of issue should be tested before it's pushed out to consumers. Honestly, it hurts the reputation of the development team and Sean Murray himself. This seems like a simple issue that should have been caught before implementation, yet it feels as though it was completely overlooked. NPC starships flying through planetary atmospheres aren't nearly as bad. The only consistent flaw Ive noticed is that theyll literally crash into mountainsides and bug out like crazy. Fortunately, this isn't a major issue since it rarely, if ever, affects the player. I understand why the crosshair locks onto prompts, but why does it need to do that for everything? For example, why does my crosshair need to stick to an NPC whos literally halfway off my screen? For resources and materials, I completely understand why that's useful. But why is it exactly the same for NPC? Once again, this feels like another oversight that should have been easy to catch and improve. For a game with one of its core pillars built around text-based interactions, it sure takes a long time to get through some of the dialogue. Most games that rely heavily on text provide an option to fast-forward through lengthy conversations. Not this game. Some of these interactions are absolutely abysmal to sit through. I'm all for lore and deep dives into a masterpiece, but I don't need a 200-page autobiography dumped on me at every trading station, especially when it's unskippable. Both random freighter encounters and pirate attacks also become annoyingly frequent. When you're first starting your journey, theyre great. You receive plenty of resources that help you progress and establish yourself in the game. However, once you're hundreds of hours into a save, its completely unnecessary to have freighters constantly requesting help during pirate attacks or spawning simply so you can purchase their frigates. Believe it or not, these encounters become extremely repetitive and frustrating. Every time youre trying to explore, youre interrupted. Why punish the player for doing exactly what the game is designed around? NPC on freighters, your crew members, are little more than the equivalent of flies buzzing around your head. Theyll shove you around because of their pathing and don't really do anything besides pace back and forth. I couldnt care less that they don't actually serve a meaningful purpose, but when they're able to physically interfere with the player, it becomes a noticeable problem. I just love being pushed around and blocked by my own crew while trying to accomplish something on my freighter. Frigates are incompetent, annoying pests that would rather waste the players time than simply do what they were assigned to do in the first place. Why does my gameplay need to be interrupted every thirty minutes for something that should be handled by the very Frigate fleet I assigned to it? It constantly pulls me away from whatever I'm doing, and not in a fun or engaging way. It also doesnt help that some content is effectively locked behind these forced, timed missions that must be completed in a very specific way, or youll never receive the reward, even after hundreds of hours. Attempting to obtain the Dream Aerial is one example of this. Im all for games that require players to grind for rewards, whether through skill progression, loot progression, or other meaningful systems. But the grind needs to be enjoyable. Constantly being nagged about things I clearly shouldn't have to micromanage is both infuriating and disrespectful of the player's time. The base-building mechanics are absolutely atrocious. The snapping system is clearly unrefined, building optimizations are practically nonexistent, and bases often fail to protect you from the outside environment. I think this system needs significant work. That said, I also understand how difficult modular building systems can be to develop and how challenging it is to optimize base building in an open-world game. This is one area where I can understand the difficulty behind the system, even if I still think it needs a significant amount of refinement. But perhaps one of the biggest contradictions in the game comes from exploration itself. For a game built entirely around exploration in a universe-sized open-world sandbox, youre punished far too heavily for exploring. Galaxy jumps destroy every upgrade module installed in your multi-tool, starship, and exosuit. It's insane that this is even a game mechanic. Why would you punish players for exploring in a game whose entire identity revolves around exploration? In my opinion, this is another major oversight that's significant enough to damage the games reputation. And that's really the problem I keep coming back to. This game is built around exploration, yet so many of its systems seem designed to interrupt, punish, or otherwise inconvenience you while you're doing exactly that. The story, however, is outstanding. The only thing I could ask for is more, but only if it's more lore, not more mechanics. We dont need another multi-tool upgrade, exocraft, or starship. We need meaningful lore additions that make us feel like we're experiencing this masterpiece for the first time again. That can only be achieved by expanding and refining the systems already in place, not by endlessly adding new ones. At this point, I dont think the game needs more things to do nearly as much as it needs the things that already exist to work better. Thats why this criticism is coming from a place of genuine appreciation rather than hatred. I dont want to see this game fail. I don't want to see it abandoned. And I certainly dont want to see everything thats already been accomplished ignored. I want to see it refined. However, if Sean Murray and the development team want to maintain the incredible reputation theyve earned, the game desperately needs refinement. Until that happens, I unfortunately can't recommend it as being worth the time or money. Out of the ten main game mechanics I discussed, only two were positive. That honestly saddens me. This game is a masterpiece, yet some flaws seem to have been ignored to the point that they diminish the experience for players who are simply playing the game as intended. Thats what makes these problems so frustrating. Im not criticizing a game that I dislike. I'm criticizing a game that I genuinely love and believe could be so much better. If you really want to experience this game for yourself, I recommend waiting for a sale instead of paying full price. At its current price, the flaws may leave you disappointed despite everything the game does exceptionally well. I don't think Ill ever truly hate this game. But I do think it deserves far better.

The most important positive is the depth of the game. This many hours in, and I still feel like I've only scratched the surface of what's possible. CONS I will say, it does feel empty. If you're looking for social immersion or a feeling of role play from the NPCs, NMS will probably disappoint you. Planets are somehow diverse and samey. Biomes are gorgeous, but somehow all contain the same resources, collected with the same methods, each and every time.

Dear No Man's Sky, I'm sorry. I said you were repetitive. I complained about the endgame. I mocked you for confusing gravity with air drag. Then I left you for Star Citizen. They hurt me. They greeted me with bugs, broken navigation, server crashes, outdated tutorials, and UI design that was invented to test human patience. Suddenly, I realized what I had. You always let me take off. You always let me land. You never made me watch a 20-minute tutorial just to figure out where to put power in my ship. You respected my time. Please... take me back. No Man's Sky has long been one of my favorite games. It's a space exploration, survival game, where you start off on a single planet filled with beautiful sights given the simple task of repairing your starship, only to find you're only on one of the many stunning planets in your star system, and that system is also one of the infinitely-many systems in the game. You get to explore, see new planets, new star-system types, spend tens to hundreds of hours doing just that because really it's hard to run out of new things to see, or you can explore these worlds and look for your quintessential starship, mine resources and earn enough money to get the upgrades you want for it to make it perfect, upgrade it and make it better, etc. And once you're done with your starship, there are still a plethora of things to do. You can do the same thing with your multi-tool, which is the thing that allows you to mine, fish, and do combat - yes there's combat in the game too - in the game. Once you're done with that, you could go and interact with the other lifeforms and yes they exist too. You could start learning their language and finally be able to understand them, or make your relationship with their race better by doing quests for them or giving them gifts... and even then you're far from finished. There's a solid base building system in the game as well, so you can build your own very base/home too, potentially after spending many hours finding the perfect planet to build it on. Done that? Well I forgot to talk about just how cool each of these worlds could be. There are many different species of animals and many many different plants and minerals on each of these wonderful planets. Each of them also has a unique atmosphere, weather, climate and ecosystem, and a different set of hazardous things too. You could then find some ocean worlds and get to see and explore an underwater world as well... I can't possibly name every thing there is in the game. There's just so much to do, and the sweet part is that the developers, even after 10 years, refuse to stop adding more wonderful content to the game, and they work hard to keep the game alive by new updates and expeditions - which are limited time events. Oh and did I mention the game is a shared-world experience? You could play with friends yes and that's just one side of it, the other one is that you can go to the worlds the other players discovered, see the bases they've built, go to the nexus space station to see the others carrying out tasks and doing things, and because of that, I find that the entire game somewhat paradoxically (because of the infinitely large world) feels very alive sometimes. Now frankly, I've kept finding the co-op portion of the game lacking considerably (which was made better after they added big starships you could ride with your friends), and connectivity problems were plenty for me as well, but one could say the developers more than make up for that in other aspects. Oh and did I talk about the story? From a technical point of view, the story wasn't the best-narrated one in the gaming world. Every dialogue is written in texts and you have to read them which is very lame and boring. BUT, personally, I really really connected with it. It might be just me, but I found the plot of the game very philosophically complex and deep. The game definitely does have a story, and I would say it is a very well thought one and it just deeply resonates with me. But I again will say that that's not something many people say and it might just be me. TL;DR, it's an awesome game. If you love exploration or survival open world games, I seriously implore you to give this game a try, or if you're hesitating to pay money for it, at least check its gameplay out on YouTube to see how it is :D

I got into this game when Multiplayer was first added. Even at the time, some years after release, it was rough around the edges. World generation could be messy, collision issues happened not infrequently. The world felt empty and lonely, which was atmospheric, but not an ideal constant. I watched as freighters were added, fixed, changed, the entire building system for them reworked. I watched the Nexus, the main player hub today, but only a story location at the time, grow from only a few mostly empty rooms, to what it is now, sometimes in big leaps, sometimes in small changes. Each addition to the game, an anticipated mechanic or bug fix, almost always paired with new content, new hand crafted things to explore and learn about. Over the time I have played this game, it has grown with and directly reciprocated the love of its fanbase. And through all of this, I feel there has been artistic integrity to the core themes and underlying meaning behind its story. This game is beautiful, and while it had a rough start mechanically, the developers have poured so much time and passion into it, and made it one of the best games I have ever played.

I am honestly completely amazed. This game was made for people like me - enjoying exploration. The ingame universe is wide wide open and unimaginably huge thanks to procedural generation, so you can spend a lot of fun time flying around from one planet system to another, searching for unexplored planets and making snapshots of wildlife you encounter. Planets that you were the first to set foot on and make a stamp on it for all other players to come after you! And taking pictures of wildlife that you encountered first! Finally a gameplay that goes beyond "see stuff, shoot stuff". You can not only fly your own spaceship, you can build one. Or two. Or more. You can either put together a quick small fighter that you build from 4 parts from other spaceships you encounter or you go the next step and design your own Corvette from scratch - piece by piece from the landing gear through thrusters and wing parts up to cockpit and interior design. You want a real huge one, made from countless parts? Go for it! Build your own Enterprise? Well, you won't be the first one to try to copy this particular ship design but go for it, maybe yours is better! Or bigger. Or more saucersome. And of course, for those who get bored too easily, there are many other facets of the gameplay that you may want to focus on instead. Want some of that pew-pew? Go hunt some pirates. Want some special thrill and adrenaline in your venes? Set your setting to extra difficult and perma-death. And when you eventually need a break and want to have some chill time building that awesome huge habitat on that paradise planet you found, you can set your game to creative and enjoy concentrating on where to put your solar panels, instead of how to get them. Honestly, an amazing piece of work, huge thumbs up to the devs. Of course, there are some things that need polish (we need a search feature and list settings options in discoveries and teleport destination list and what is up with the light cubes colors? Is this gonna be fixed? Why is getting off a ladder midway so complicated? Can we get elevators instead?) Because when there's a ton of interesting things to do, there's bound to be a ton times two ideas how to improve or what to add, but overall this is finally a game that I can call perfect - at least definitely perfect for me. Oh and btw I am playing on a complete potato. I bought this game not knowing if it will work out as I have like half of the minimum requirements but I heard the game was optimised to be a bit more accessible and after watching some videos how to make it work on low spec hardware, I gave it a try. And here I am, currently on my 4th base and 2nd corvette build... It works!

It's a good game, but definitely a mixed bag: I'd say the core gameplay loop is immensely satisfying, but the game also lacks depth and the mechanics are largely hit or miss. There are some serious oversights that have surprisingly remained unfixed for years and I don't think there's any plan to make those changes any time soon. As an example, resource gathering using tools in this game is absolutely phenomenal. The mining laser is one of the most satisfying mechanics I've ever used in any adjacent title: it feels so good to be able to mine from a great distance and have all the materials simply appear in your inventory. The terrain manipulation tool is also satisfying to use and it has a lot of potential combat and exploration uses as well. But I'd say a lot of the movement mechanics in the game really are not up to par at all. The jetpack feels tremendously clunky and the rocket boots' trigger far too often in response to double pressing space, even with large time gaps in between. Gathering items by holding e can be painfully slow, but at least you can keep moving while doing so. The game doesn't do a good job of selecting the correct item when you're up close and personal, unfortunately: you'd think that it would default to the closest object based on your camera, but it instead uses your players' position. These mechanics extend to conversations, shops, entering and exiting your ship as well as utilizing tools like autopilot. A lot of commands that you would think should have an easily avaiable shortcut do not and the constant short delays get old really quick. Of course, that's not to say that there's anything worth having in any of the conversations you do have, because NPCs have effectively nothing meaningful to say. Gathering words is immensely satisfying if you're into collecting, but the reward is to have a few more throwaway lines of dialogue that don't change from system to system, and will likely just be skipped anyway as you mash 1 repeatedly to learn a new word from the next NPC. Storage can be quite obnoxious, especially when you just start out and have next to no inventory slots: the problem can be fixed to some extent, but I still don't see what the value is in having arbitrary limits to storage in a game that's supposed to be all about exploring and seeing what's out there: infinite storage space and slots in your exosuit would be a great addition so that you don't get bogged down by inventory management and base building The exploration is pretty deceptive, too: you'd think that the game would be all about exploring, but there isn't really much to explore. Everything: the planets, systems, galaxies, creatures, etc.. function in effectively the exact same way regardless of where you are in the universe, so there isn't much to look forward to regarding exploration. At some point the illusion clears and you see that there's effectively nothing meaningful to look forward to. The breadth of content is immense, though, and if you enjoy collecting and base building then you'll probably find the later stages of the game more than satisfactory. There are an enormous amount of technologies, structures, and tools that you have at your disposal within bases: I just don't find this aspect of the game particularly enjoyable. For the general playerbase, there is progress to be made concerning player power, acquiring better ships, and building up your "hub" ships but I just don't think it's enough of an incentive for me to continue, so I'm dropping the game. That being said, I did enjoy my experience despite coming to the conclusion that it was an immensely shallow one.

It's been a few months since I started playing [b]No Man's Sky[/b], and now I think I've experienced enough of the game to leave a review. No Man's Sky is a very unique, vast and ambitious game; I'll go over some of the main core aspects, to explain what I like and what I don't. [h3] Exploration [/h3] The bread and butter of No Man's Sky is exploration; unfortunatly, this is where I think the game is too ambitious for its own good. At first, exploring planets, space stations and ships is pretty fun, but soon it becomes quite repetitive; the game simply doesn't have enough "templates" for the procedural generation: - most planets feel too similar to each other; - every space station is pretty much the same; - there's a lack of places of interest. The ability to name pretty much everything you come across is an interesting and cool system; exploring is also quite rewarding in terms of resources. Every now and then it is possible to find a memorable planet that feels like no other. [h3] Travelling [/h3] What I personally feel like the game does very well is travelling: space truly feels huge; land vehicles are slow and kind of weird to use, but the spaceships are amazing in pretty much every way: driving them, their design, the ability to create and customize a ship from scratch (especially corvettes!). My biggest gripe with ships, apart from certain weird restrictions while building them, is the combat. While the ship weapons feel pretty fun, fighting other ships is pretty much always the same thing: press the lock button and shoot. It's not too bad, but it does become repetitive and it feels too simple. [h3] Survival [/h3] Another important aspect of No Man's Sky is surviving in the often extreme conditions you find yourself in: toxic, radioactive, extreme temperature planets are everywhere; the mechanics of survival are, actually, very simple and basic. It often just involves collecting a resource to recharge your equipment (for example, oxygen for life support). Depending on the chosen gamemode, this can be a mild inconvenience or something to look out for constantly. Personally, I feel indifferent to these systems: on one hand, they feel necessary for the game, on the other they aren't particularly fun/exciting; I guess they're fine. [h3] Technology and Multi-tool [/h3] To help you survive, your equipment, exosuit and vehicles can be upgraded through tech; and there is a lot of different tech that can be found/bought. Some simply improve the efficiency of your multi-tool (your main way to gather resources and to fight on land), others can even unlock travel to more complex systems. The multi-tool is pretty reliable, and even if land combat is pretty boring, the amount of tech and weapons that can be used is great. These mechanics make the overall progression of the game far more interesting and fun. [h3] Story [/h3] The story in No Man's Sky is not the center piece, and as such, it tries to move out the way pretty quickly. Despite this, I enjoyed it; one thing which I also didn't mind but many people may find weird is the way dialogue is done; I'm not sure how to explain it, but it's very descriptive. It tries to "tell more than show". [h3] Other stuff [/h3] One of the most unique aspects of No Man's Sky is the way multiplayer works: it's not really an MMO, but there is a main hub, and everytime you enter a new system, you could meet another player there. Of course, due to the scale of the game, this is very rare, and everything multiplayer-related can be turned off in the settings. Now, while trying to play with friends, I came across a few bugs causing some of us to getting disconnected; this is part of a bigger problem: there are quite a lot of bugs and glitches. I haven't met any game-breaking bugs, but most of them were related to the terrain and base building. So, what is my opinion on No Man's Sky? While the game suffers from a lot of problems, and many mechanics just don't feel complete, it is still an entertaining game that is unlike anything else I have ever played; I also appreciate all the work the developers have been doing in the past years, pretty much for free. I am very happy of my experience, and had quite a lot of fun, so I recommend it.

I have to admit, No Man’s Sky does have something special going for it. That said, there’s a very strong chance I’ll never play it again. For anyone desperate for a massive space game filled with collecting, scanning, building, and seamless exploration with friends, I can absolutely see the appeal. Flying directly off one planet, through space, and landing somewhere completely different was genuinely impressive. The tutorial was a nightmare for my ADHD because it throws a ridiculous amount of information and systems at you. To its credit, it does try to explain everything. Do not rush through it like I did. You need to slow down, read carefully, and actually understand what each glowing box is teaching you. My biggest problem was the combat. If I’m exploring a galaxy filled with completely different planets and ecosystems, I want hostile creatures and some actual danger. Instead, the ground combat felt like an afterthought. Headshots did not even register. My laser literally passed through creatures’ heads without detecting a hitbox. C'mon. What game does not give a head a hitbox? The overwhelming systems and lacklustre combat completely killed my desire to continue. I hate space-themed games and need some kind of combat challenge to stay engaged, so this clearly was not made for me. I understand the hype. I just do not share it.

So this is a mid 2026 review and I don't know about the launch era fiasco at all, so I will not address anything like that or what updates were happened along the years. Although I have mixed feelings about this game. While it is truly incredible to have such an infinite amount of scale to explore both inwards and outwards, the game is not that realistic when it comes to the real universe. It feels like I'm watching the universe throughout some Disneyland sunglasses. Life is not that common in the universe as this game shows, and it is way more hostile in both planetary and in both organism wide. This all coming together with the mechanisms, the systems and the overall playstyles the game can offer, you will either end up with the most boring game of your life, or you will end up with the most endless fun time of your life. I am somehow fell between these two. So while I incredibly enjoy this game, the scale and the true exploration aspect of it, I somehow find it repetitive and shallow after some time. So I play this occasionally picking up and putting it aside for some time over and over... If there would be a neutral review button for this game, I would gladly choose it, but there isn't so I will stick with recommended, as it would be unfair to state otherwise. But, it would be also unfair to state that go ahead and buy it now, so here is the deal: If you like space exploration, grind, trading and mining resources, building structures buy it. If you are looking for a story, characters, or any narrative, or just for a realistic universe, don't buy it. I feel like there is no middle way. 8/10 recommended

TL;DR - You're safe to ignore the hype with this one. Some good ideas on offer but it's too fiddly to be relaxing and not interesting enough to be exciting. It also has - and I'm not joking when I say this - the worst gamepad implementation I've ever seen in a PC game. There's a HUGE deadzone, and no way to fix it ingame. I will never understand why this game gets glazed so hard. It still feels unfinished. -------------------------- Claims to be a game where you can explore the world and build bases. Exploring consists of 50% exploring, 30% harvesting, 20% wasting time because of the time-wasting UI design. Stuff that should take one or two clicks/presses is instead put in nested menus. You can build bases, they reckon. The base I built used less than 50 pieces, and yet it failed to even appear in game consistently. Sometimes the roof was missing. Other times two whole walls were missing. The game's flight is horribly floaty, and the gamepad control input has a ridiculous deadzone problem that cannot be fixed ingame. At the price these cretins charge, the least they could do is sort out a gamepad slider or two for their customers. This is one of those games that explains how to do stuff but rarely why, which leads me to my next point. The amount of time wasted is just laughable. In a normal game you'd open a container and collect an item. In No Man's Sky, you have to do all kinds of crap first. Sometimes you have to remove rust from the container, but you can't just use the container after that, you have to exit the container and then click on it again. Sometimes you have to read a bunch of completely irrelevant crap before you're allowed to use the container. That sums the game up perfectly, right there. It tries to be immersive but it keeps tripping over its own feet trying to be clever and failing at every step of the way. 'I am 14 and space is deep': The game. Imagine you pick up a piece of poo off the ground, throw it at a stranger, and then yell '10 POINTS!'. Are you playing with poo, or are you playing a game? What a strange question. What a strange game.

After putting this game off my backlog for half a decade, I finally had an urge to boot it up. I have almost played this game at least a little bit every single day ever since. After a couple months I've hit around half a thousand hours give or take. This is a fantastic space exploration game + survival game. Visiting various planets becomes a bit repetitive after your first, oh i dunno 2 or 3 dozen. The points of interest get looped and reused after a certain point but getting to that point takes a fair bit of time, it's mildly forgivable for that reason. Collecting ships, the grind for parts and upgrades, more multi-tools, learning of new mechanics that were added in the years of updates this game gets, it's hard to imagine this was the same game I saw get "released" a full 10 years ago. Had I not known the story behind Hello Games, I would have never even gotten this game on sale years ago where it would sit in my Steam library for so long, only to be finally picked up this year. Many people lazily compare this game to "Minecraft, but in space" but personally I feel it's more akin to "Valheim, but in space" with the urge to build F.O.B.s every 5 or so jumps, the progression of metal ores, and general feeling of exploring an unknown and empty realm. The game is often touted as this amazing feat, where the fact that the in-game universe is so big and so massive that we wouldn't be able to explore it all. While it's impressive, I feel the real strong feeling the game instills is giving you a little pocket of the universe you get to explore, and every now and then you can sometimes see a system or planet that was discovered by another player months, years, or sometimes just weeks prior to you. The game's repetition really hits after a few hundred hours, and once you beat the story along with most other new added content via free updates, it's easy to see how people get bored of this game. Granted, they're getting bored after hundreds and hundreds of hours, so I feel that's not a big deal for this kind of game. Sometimes they're not engaging with all available content, such as the creature arena (never do PvP, you're either going up against little timmy with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or you're up against Super Mega CTC with a hacked and impossible moveset involving stalling with HP absorb shields and stuns in a game with no PP system like Pokemon), the expeditions, etc. This game has lots of things to offer, but it's very possible to do it all before the thousand-hour mark. If you're looking for a forever game, this is not it, you will be dropping this game in and out of your rotation over time. However, it always will come back if you enjoy it due to how frequent this game gets free content updates and all the expeditions that are to come. This game is massively worth it, even more-so on sale.

[h1]The Greatest Comeback in Gaming[/h1][hr][/hr][b]No Man’s Sky[/b] is almost unrecognizable compared to the game I bought on release day. My best friend and I rushed to GameStop because we wanted to know if we could meet in the universe and what was waiting at the center of the galaxy. Back then, there was no real multiplayer. And after hours of travelling to the center, you were simply thrown into another galaxy and had to start again. It was one of the biggest disappointments I had ever experienced in gaming. But Hello Games kept going. Every year brought new updates, new systems and more content. Multiplayer, base building, expeditions, settlements, freighters, better space combat and huge visual upgrades. There is so much in the game now that it can honestly feel overwhelming. No Man’s Sky went from broken promises to one of the biggest redemption stories in gaming.[hr][/hr][i]They actually fixed the impossible.[/i]

Sadly a disappointing game. The story forces you to care about a character with almost no build up. The entire storyline is just "how do i risk my life to save this person i just met?" And yet the story acts like you're their long lost wife. It also forcse yo uto go to the public hub just so another NPC can go "I don't care", and send you back out to whoever knows where. Along with that, it's a lot of "go to generated structure A, go to hub, go to generated structure B" and repeat. Gameplay-wise, there's things to do, but no real incentive to do it. There's progressions of star types, but no real reason to go to them other than materials. The way you get stronger is either getting upgrades for your equipment, or by buying new equipment for classes. Not to mention the optimization. I can't actually play in VR, even when I have decent PC specs. I uninstalled and refunded it right after, but after watching more videos I gave it the benefit of the doubt and rebought it. It wasn't worth it. This game has few things to do, with so little reason of doing it. Sometimes it feels like it's just random activities just taped onto the game (e.g the Pokemon stuff). If you wanted a game that was expansive not just in it's planets, but in activities and generated structures, this is not the game.

NMS is amazing. It's expansive; you can really carve out a piece of the universe and make it your own. You can customize your corvette, your freighter, your planet, your system, your base, your outfit, your weapon. The stories are cute and do a good job at driving your progress through the various unlock trees and game mechanics. Flight controls are restrictive and... cute. Hold S to keep aiming at your enemy, press leftclick to shoot. I've never died in this game and I've also stopped dodging - there is no challenge even if the game does a good job making it feel like there is. I empowered my suit and weapon because I wanted things to go faster, or just to collect "all S class" gear, but not that it was needed. Let's get one thing straight though; this is NOT a multiplayer game in the sense that you can play WITH your friends. You can play alongside them, but this is also limited greatly by the game's ability to synchronize with a slower back end system. The best you can do with your friend is a pokemon battle. Everything else either fails at the slightest desync or is for your eyes alone (even when you're standing next to each other). No Man's Sky is a space sim, sandbox. It has almost an infinite variety of difficulty settings allowing different levels of most of the game's survival aspects. The difficulty can range from pure creative mode with no damage or costs involved to extreme survival with permadeath. There is even an "abandoned" mode, where you are the only intelligent life in the universe. This adds an extra level of survival mechanics to the game, as alien life forms are one of the means of acquiring necessary resources in NMS. In the abandoned mode there is no story to follow currently, Perhaps Hello Games will ad this someday in the future. I hope they do as, this would add some goals to work toward, and perhaps some unique achievements. The systems and planets to visit are too innumerable to see them all. However, once you've seen each of the biomes, "you've seen them all". This doesn't mean that every planet is one of five or six varieties and there is no point to see more than one. The different survival mechanics are mixed and matched in the biomes, as well as the flora and fauna. So, each planet seems somewhat unique to the others you've visited. You can create multiple saves on your account. I believe there is a limit, but I haven't hit it...although I tend to delete most saves after I complete the story. Having said that, no two playthroughs will be identical even if you complete the story on each. So multiple saves can still be fun to play, especially if you tinker with the difficulty settings. There is a cooperative aspect to the game. Although this is not as robust as most of the other games I've played. Coop is only really good on space station missions and Nexus missions, and not really in the story line gameplay or on expeditions. Expeditions should definitely be geared toward coop play. HG/Sean, if you're reading this, please consider making the entire game geared toward coop, you know...the way Light No Fire is supposed to be. I keep coming back to the game after taking a break. So, I would say that all in all you can't go wrong by trying No Man's Sky.

~ DIFFICULTY ~ 🔲 My 90 year old grandma could play it 🔲 Easy ✅ Normal 🔲 Hard 🔲 Dark Souls ~ GRAPHICS ~ 🔲 MS Paint 🔲 Bad 🔲 Meh 🔲 Graphics dont matter in this game ✅ Good 🔲 Beautiful ~ MUSIC ~ 🔲 Bad 🔲 Not special 🔲 Good ✅ Eargasm ~ STORY ~ 🔲 This game has no story 🔲 Like playing Temple Runners for the story ✅ It's there for the people who want it 🔲 Well written 🔲 Epic story ~ PRICE ~ 🔲 Free 🔲 Underpriced ✅ Perfect Price 🔲 Could be cheaper 🔲 Overpriced 🔲 Complete waste of money ~ REQUIREMENTS ~ 🔲 You can run it on a microwave ✅ Average 🔲 High end 🔲 NASA computer ~ LENGTH ~ 🔲 Very Short (0 - 3 hours) 🔲 Short (3 - 15 hours) 🔲 Average (15-50 hours) 🔲 Long (50-90 hours) ✅ Extremely long (90-110 hours) 🔲 No ending ~ FUN ~ 🔲 I'd rather watch paint dry 🔲 Hard to enjoy ✅ Repetitive 🔲 Actually pretty amusing 🔲 Ride of your life ~ REPLAYABILITY~ 🔲 It's a one-time experience 🔲 Only for achievements 🔲 If you wait a few months/years 🔲 Definitely ✅ Infinitely replayable ~ WORTH BUYING ~ 🔲 No 🔲 Wait for sale ✅ Yes ---------------- No Man's Sky delivers an ambitious and expansive space exploration experience that has grown significantly since its original release. With an almost limitless universe to discover, the game constantly rewards curiosity through exploration, survival, crafting, and discovery. Its impressive scale is matched by a steady stream of content that provides players with countless opportunities to forge their own adventure. Rather than following a heavily scripted narrative, the game presents a mysterious journey centred around ancient civilisations, strange anomalies, and the secrets of the universe. The story unfolds gradually through exploration and encounters with various alien races, encouraging players to piece together its lore at their own pace. While the narrative may feel understated compared to traditional role-playing games, it successfully complements the game's emphasis on freedom and discovery. Gameplay offers remarkable variety, combining planetary exploration, resource gathering, crafting, trading, base building, and space combat into one cohesive experience. Every planet introduces different environments, wildlife, and hazards, ensuring exploration rarely feels repetitive despite the game's enormous scale. Multiplayer features and regular updates have further expanded the experience, giving players even more ways to collaborate and explore together. Visually, No Man's Sky creates a colourful and imaginative universe filled with breathtaking landscapes and unique planetary ecosystems. Procedurally generated worlds often produce stunning vistas, ranging from lush forests to hostile frozen wastelands and vibrant alien oceans. The atmospheric lighting, detailed spacecraft, and impressive visual effects combine to create an immersive science fiction setting that remains captivating throughout extended play sessions. Overall, No Man's Sky succeeds in delivering one of the most expansive exploration games available, supported by years of meaningful improvements and additional content. Although certain mechanics can become repetitive over time and the story remains relatively subtle, the sheer freedom, creativity, and sense of discovery consistently outweigh these shortcomings. Players seeking a vast sandbox filled with exploration, construction, and adventure will find an engaging experience that continues to evolve long after the journey begins. No Man's Sky gets a 8/10. No Man’s Sky is gaming’s greatest redemption story. Launching in 2016 to intense criticism, Hello Games spent a decade delivering massive, entirely free overhauls. Today, it stands as a breathtakingly deep, definitive space-faring sandbox. The pure magic begins when you fix your starter ship, blast through the atmosphere, and realize you can seamlessly fly to any star with zero loading screens. The procedural universe features a staggering 18 quintillion planets across 256 unique galaxies, teeming with custom biomes and complex dynamic weather systems. What makes it truly legendary is the sheer variety of playstyles. You can play as a lonely cosmic explorer cataloging alien wildlife, an industrialist constructing automated factories, or a space pirate raiding freighters. Content updates have completely transformed the gameplay loop, introducing pilotable capital freighters, customizable heavy land trucks, a physics-manipulating gravity gun module, and Pokémon-style monster-battling holo-arenas. While the sheer volume of mechanics can feel incredibly overwhelming for newcomers in the first few hours, the game excels by letting you completely ignore the main quests to forge your own path. It is an absolute masterpiece of survival, crafting, and cosmic wonder.

I have exactly 26 hours in No Man's Sky, which means I'm still in the honeymoon phase where every new planet makes me whisper, "What fresh nonsense is this?" I bought this game expecting majestic space exploration. Instead, I've become a full-time gravel enthusiast with an unhealthy emotional attachment to ferrite dust. The gameplay loop is a tractor beam aimed directly at your free time. "I just need some carbon." Three hours later... "I've adopted an alien pet that looks like a rotisserie chicken with antlers, purchased a suspiciously expensive starship, and completely forgotten why I left my base." Every planet feels like it was designed by an alien intern five minutes before the deadline. "Here's a paradise world." Acid rain. "Never mind." The wildlife is incredible. I've scanned animals that look like someone emptied an IKEA warehouse into an evolutionary blender. Half the creatures have too many legs, the other half look deeply offended that I exist. My only complaint? For a game containing 18 quintillion planets, the galaxy is suffering from a catastrophic shortage of premium gooner game material. You're telling me I can discover sentient plasma clouds, living starships, robot companions, pirate armadas, and cosmic horrors beyond human comprehension... ...but the dating pool consists of three species whose resting facial expression is "tax audit." The Gek look like they collect coupons. The Vy'keen look like they'd challenge me to mutual combat for making eye contact. The Korvax are literally elegant kitchen appliances. The universe is beautiful. The universe is lonely. Sean Murray, if you're reading this, give us one impossibly charismatic space pirate who flirts outrageously and then immediately steals my warp fuel. That's all I'm asking. That said, I completely understand why people have 2,000+ hours. This game has weaponized curiosity. Every destination leads to five more destinations until you've accidentally sacrificed your entire Saturday to collecting minerals you'll never use. 10/10. Came for the exploration. Stayed because my dopamine receptors now activate whenever I discover another weird little moon with glowing grass and absolutely zero respectable gooner opportunities.

I've played a lot of games over the years, but No Man's Sky is one of the greatest comeback stories in gaming history. What started as a good idea has evolved into an absolutely massive universe filled with endless exploration, base building, space combat, trading, and multiplayer adventures. The amount of content the developers have added for free is incredible. Every update brings something new, whether it's discovering strange new planets, building your dream settlement, commanding a fleet of freighters, or simply relaxing while exploring beautiful alien worlds. There is always something to do, and no two journeys ever feel the same. What really makes No Man's Sky special is the sense of wonder. Landing on a new planet and not knowing what you'll find never gets old. The game rewards curiosity and lets you play however you want—explorer, trader, pirate, builder, or scientist. Huge credit to the team at Hello Games for never giving up on this game and continuing to support it years after release. No Man's Sky isn't just a game anymore—it's an ever-expanding universe that keeps getting better with every update. 10/10 – A masterpiece of exploration and one of the best redemption stories in gaming.

[h1][b]From Zero to 320 Hours – My Absolute Favorite Space Adventure![/b][/h1] I'm not your typical "hardcore" gamer who buys every new release. I choose games like good books: I look at the description, the overall vibe, and I strictly avoid spoilers because I believe in the magic of blind discovery. When I got my laptop back in 2022, GTA V was our first go-to game with friends (clocked 315 hours, but the hype eventually died down, we played for 2-3 years), followed by Sea of Thieves in Autumn 2023, which we still boot up occasionally for some fun treasure hunts (I have 250 hours in it). But then came the first week of December 2025, and I bought No Man's Sky. What happened next completely caught me off guard. I put 120 hours into the game in just two weeks—this universe completely consumed me. Now, barely half a year later, it has become my most-played game with 320 hours, and the most important part: [b]I haven’t been bored for a single second![/b] This officially pushes it to the absolute top of my Top 3 most-played games, right ahead of GTA V and Sea of Thieves. [h2][b]🚀 The "Fun" Part is Just Beginning![/b][/h2] I’ve finally reached the point where I actually understand the mechanics inside out. I know what to look for, where to go, and how everything works. In a way, the true, sandbox community experience is just opening up for me now: [list] [*][b]Base Building:[/b] I can finally start designing my own [b][i]monumental bases[/i][/b]. [*][b]Achievements:[/b] Time to hunt down and max out those [b][i]Steam trophies[/i][/b]. [*][b]Galactic Exploration:[/b] Smoothly exploring planets at my own comfortable pace. [/list] I also have to highlight the [b][i]Expeditions[/i][/b]. Right now, I'm playing [b][i]The Swarm[/i][/b], which is the first live event I’ve been able to participate in. It’s a genius move by the developers: just when the normal gameplay loop slows down a bit, an Expedition drops and completely revitalizes the entire experience! [h2][b]🪐 Final Verdict: At its Peak After 10 Years[/b][/h2] I know the general history of the game and the rocky road it took to get here. Now, celebrating its 10th anniversary in 2026, No Man's Sky has officially delivered exactly what was promised in that initial grand vision. If you've been hesitating to buy it, [h3][b]NOW is the absolute perfect time to jump in![/b][/h3] I see massive potential for the future; Hello Games keeps bringing fresh updates, and I'm sure they will add even more content down the line. To me, this game is a massive positive surprise and an absolute masterpiece.

No Man's Sky is a game with one of the biggest redemption stories in video game history. When it launched in 2016, it was a massive disappointment. The game was far from what the developers promised, and it got heavily criticized. But Hello Games did not give up. They kept working on it, releasing regular and often huge updates completely for free. Over the years, they turned a project that was practically written off into one of the best space sandbox games ever made. It is a perfect example of how a studio should treat its game, and many others could learn from them. The game itself is set in an almost infinite procedurally generated universe with over 18 quintillion planets. Every planet is different, offering a wide range of environments to explore. You can find water planets, planets with no colors, planets with extreme storms, and many more. The variety keeps exploration fresh, and you never really know what you will find next. The gameplay systems are very well done. Every upgrade you get actually feels meaningful, and you notice the difference. There is also a great building system that lets you create bases anywhere, from mountain tops to deep underwater. You can play the game in co-op with friends, which makes the experience even better. The game also regularly features expeditions, which are timed community events with unique objectives and exclusive rewards. During these, you play together with thousands of other players, which creates a great sense of community. No Man's Sky is incredibly addictive, especially if you are the type of person who needs some linearity to stay focused, but then ends up doing a million other things anyway. You can easily sink thousands of hours into it. There is always something to do. You can explore planets, trade with alien races, hunt pirates, go fishing, build bases, manage a fleet, or just follow the main story. The game lets you find what you enjoy and just do that. TLDR; No Man's Sky went from a broken mess at launch to one of the best space games ever thanks to years of free updates. It offers endless exploration, many activities, and great co-op, but its massive sandbox can feel overwhelming. [h2] Pros: [/h2] - Developers keep adding free content regularly - Incredible variety of planets to explore - Great building system - Fun to play in co-op - Regular expeditions with exclusive rewards - Very addictive - Many different activities to choose from - Every upgrade feels meaningful [h2] Cons: [/h2] - It is a huge sandbox, and the overwhelming freedom can be too much for some players [h1] Overall rating: 10/10 [/h1]
