I remember when No Man's Sky first launched, the reviews were rough and it kind of fell off my radar. Fast forward to now and what's here today feels like an almost entirely different game. At its core this is a chill exploration game. When I first started playing I found it almost addictive, there's something about the freedom and the loop of it that just hooks you. The story is decent enough, it gives you enough direction to keep things feeling purposeful. That said, it's hard to ignore that the universe can start feeling a bit samey after a while. The gameplay loop is fun, but at the end of the day it's still a loop, and once the initial wonder wears off a little it can feel a bit grindy. I don't play nearly as much as I used to and it's become more of a game I return to every now and then for a few hours rather than something I'm actively grinding through. A couple of other things worth knowing - the tutorials don't explain everything so expect to look a few things up online. Optimisation isn't its strongest suit either, I find myself having to restart every so often before performance starts to dip. Overall a genuinely good game that earned its second chance.

TLDR: Suffers greatly from feature creep and aggressive mediocrity, with strong hints of identity crisis despite ten years of effort. Stay away if you care about quality game design. It's fair if you like variety and casual grind. Imagine an Asian resturant selling meals from all over Asia without a single focus on one culture, all below standard and bastardized, but exceed with variety, and the kitchen can't stop pushing out new food until you are fed up, this is not far away from No Man's Sky. I wanted to migrate from GOG to Steam copy, clearly I've forgotten how bad this game feels, I have decided to not spent more time and money on this game due to reasons below: An overhyped game with too much focus on its redemption arc rather than it's problems. HG is game developer still stuck with minigame / mobile game mechanics mindset with the ambition of a AAA developer and the scale of AAA games, hence the strong disconnection from it's concept and execution. Postive: -Great scale and many worlds to explore, good vista if you are into casual planet exploration, where you can randomly bump into breathtaking locations. -Variety of things to do -Stable update pattern from the developer -Bytebeat - you can make music with it Negative: -The updates themselves are of questionable quality; the developer, with their short update cycle, has little incentive to make quality updates. Instead, they function as marketing campaigns to attract new buyers, instead of fixing the bug-ridden game. -It's a tech test bench of the developer's new game: Light No Fire. -Half-baked concepts that goes nowhere, many of which are borrowed cheaply from other classical Sci-Fi and games, Ex: Exocraft, Trash Truck, Cooking, Biological horror, Settlements, Derelict Feighter, Sandworm, the entire update tree of the combat system... -Features of this game: Space sim, Base building, Colony Management, Exploration with Survival, an RPG system, a single player narrative...all being throw into the mix, severely lacking synergy, focus between systems and concept in a self-proclaimed sandbox game, even the fanbase can't agree on its genre and focus. -Clunky console UI design where you have to press long confirm on everything -Absolutely atrocious multiplayer where player grief near objective is rampant and harms performance in single player. -Unable to take its strongest point, which is procedural generation to the next level, lacking variations in POIs and structure harms narrative potential. See that underwater ruin in Steam's screenshot page? You will see that again and again and again on a different planets. -AI is practically non-existent in this game, both in terms of combat AI, companion... -Static universe where nothing you do matters. -Still the worst existential story I've ever seen written

No Man’s Sky is an incredibly enjoyable game, and for me it represents one of the best examples of open-world exploration done right. The fact that there are over 250 galaxies to explore makes it feel almost endless, and there’s always something new to discover no matter how long you play. There’s also a huge amount of variety in what you can do. Base building is surprisingly deep and creative, fleet expeditions add a sense of long-term progression, and ship collecting gives you something to constantly work towards. On top of that, Hello Games regularly introduces expeditions, which give players new challenges and opportunities to earn unique rewards and collectibles. My only real issue is the performance. I experience frequent crashes, and sometimes the game will crash multiple times before I’m able to properly get into a session, which can be really frustrating. Despite that, I still find the overall experience highly enjoyable and worth recommending, especially if you enjoy exploration and sandbox-style gameplay.

This game is not what I expected at all. I normally don't like games with no real ending. I prefer progression, a clear goal, and knowing that eventually I will reach a final point and move on. Endless games usually lose me because after some time it starts feeling repetitive or directionless. But this game somehow hits differently. When I started, I thought it was just another space survival game: collect resources, build things, repeat. I wasn't expecting much. Then weird things started happening. I discovered my own star system and realized I could rename it with my IGN. Then I found out that if I upload it, other players who reach that place can actually see that I discovered it first. Suddenly the universe stopped feeling like a generated map and started feeling like a shared world. The scale of the game is hard to describe. You realize you're not exploring a small handcrafted map, you're inside something absurdly huge. The crazy thing is that the game doesn't force you into one path either. One minute I was looking for copper to repair things, the next I found a crashed B-class ship and started debating whether I should repair it, scrap it, or keep it. Then I ended up learning about salvaging, discovering planets, inventory management, and ten other things I wasn't even planning to do. What surprised me most is that there is always something pulling your curiosity forward. You constantly tell yourself: "one more thing before I stop." I'll check this planet. I'll finish this mission. I'll see what that signal is. I'll repair this ship. Then suddenly a lot more time has passed than expected. I still don't know how long I will stick with this game. Maybe I'll play for 50 hours, maybe hundreds. But I can already say this game completely changed my expectations. I expected an endless game that I would get bored of quickly. Instead I got a game that keeps making me curious. There is so much to do, but it somehow doesn't feel overwhelming. Great game.

After playing this game for many hours, I think I can finally post my thoughts on it to help out those of you skimming through these reviews right now. I'll try to make it super simple. This is NOT a survival game. If you're looking for intense space battles, heavy story telling, and meaningful character interactions? This game is not for you chief. What the game actually is: A chill, exploring, collecting and creative experience The game is "survival" in title, but once you learn the systems, and bulk up your character, nothing can touch you. There are so many upgrades you can get for your suit and ship, that the survival aspect of the game kinda fades into the background. But if you're into min/maxing your gear, its always fun to get as strong as you can and just coast. Where the game really shines, is just the absolute scope of what you can do. If you like to collect things, build things, and complete achievements, this is your game. Collect ships, weapons, critters, and cosmetics. Build bases with decorations you can earn on limited time events. Build up your ranks with different factions. All can be done without popping a nerve, or throwing a controller at your screen. I find the game to be relaxing, and I always come back for more, cause they keep adding features to try out. To this day, this is still one of my favorite games, its nice to just kick back, find some cool planets to build on, and collect as much cool stuff as my game save will allow me. Hopefully this helps you, random person on Steam. If any of this sounds appealing to you, give it a shot!

This many years in and there is still so much that was promised but only half delivered. We got living ships and organic frigates but still poor sourcing for sacs to expand the living ships, no organic equivalent to the technology we can install onto any other ship, and no living freighters. We have no way to upgrade the class on a freighter besides buy a better one if you find one. Multiple items still have no purpose or only craft a single item. They gave us corvette ships which were awesome but we still can't leave the station with a different ship without it forgetting the loadout on the corvette and we can't land them on landing pads or even default to beaming down onto a landing pad months later. If you dig with the terrain manipulator you can find voids in planetary cores that you can fall into on several planets and you pray it has an ocean so you can swim back out of it. Collision effects are still unpredictable. I have been launched into the stratosphere clipping a tree and been hung up on a portal site my ship was spawned next to in the past week. We have been given an anticlimactic end to the Atlas story chain but never offered closure to the realm of glass, the hive mother, or the augmented storylines. The best functional parts of the game are the Minotar which has had to refreshes since introduction and the freighter material beam making all of your support items easy to access regardless of which ship you leave with or even if you're on foot. I hope this coming year we will finally get a freighter refresh with living freighters, the ability to own more than one even if you can only deploy one at a time, and some sort of technology to make the living ships competitive compared to the regular ships. Despite the flaws, it's still the game I spend the most time just flying around "looking at stuff." Once you learn how the math works in game you can be really aggressive toward threats along your path. I'd still recommend this game to a friend to veg out.

On the plus side, the game is a single purchase, works even on an aging, mid-grade gaming laptop under linux, has an impressively massive open world, and progress isn't agonizingly grindy. On the minus side, the bugs are persistent, the game world is impressively static (nothing you do matters to any npc faction), very few of the gameplay concepts are fully executed, and, even though you can cross galaxies, you can't secure a load of toxic waste in the bed of a truck.

Playing No Man’s Sky for the first time in 2026 has been an incredible experience. I have never played a game with this much width and depth. I am about 100 hours in and still feel like I have barely scratched the surface of what is possible here. What stands out most is not just how much there is to do, but how deep each part of the game goes. Exploration, base building, space combat, trading, and survival systems all feel like full experiences on their own rather than side features. Every system seems to have layers that keep unfolding the more time you spend with it. There are so many things to get pulled into and lose yourself in. It is perfect if you enjoy variety and freedom in your gameplay, because there is always something new to discover, build, improve, or optimize. The sense of progression feels natural, and the game constantly rewards curiosity without forcing a single path. It is also impressive how much the game has grown and been refined over time. Because it has changed so significantly over the past decade, it can sometimes be difficult to find current, accurate information when looking things up. In a way, that makes discovery feel even more personal, since you often learn by doing rather than relying on outdated guides. Overall, it feels like a massive, living sandbox that keeps revealing more the longer you stay in it.

No Man's Sky is what you get when you attach morals to a game company. They overhyped and overpromised because they didn't have a marketing division to keep their CEO from babbling when he got nervous on camera and in front of people. They released a buggy game that wasn't even a tenth of what they had promised. But, here's where the story differs from other game releases. Hello Games went radio silent for months, and then released a patch. It fixed bugs, and gave some more content. And it was free. Ten years later, and countless additional updates, all free, and they have made one of the most beloved games on Steam. Now, about the game? It's great. There's hundreds of hours of things to do. If you get bored, make a new game with new universe rules. Think it's easy baby-time game? Turn on survival mode. Still too easy, you masochist you? Turn permadeath on. You can look up what the expeditions did, and do your own expedition based on that until an actual expedition rolls around. Hunt for fun pets, and then arena fight them pocket monster style. Build ridiculous monuments to man's folly. Roleplay as a galactic trucker, hauling freight from system to system, building up profitable trade routes based on maximizing profit while minimizing risk. Which means you need to map out a trade route that hits a bunch of three star economies while avoiding two and three star aggression systems. You can even become a planetary garbageman, slowly but surely cleaning up a planet. Basically, if you get bored in No Man's Sky, then you lack imagination. Hello Games has handed you a beautiful and expansive set of multiverses for you to explore and build in. Basically, imagine Starfield, but made by a game company with moral fiber. They didn't just crap out a buggy game, and then expect the modding community to fix it. Like Bethesda does with ALL of their games.

THE GOOD: Very fun, relaxing game. It kinda feels like Minecraft in space in the sense that there is A LOT of stuff to do, but there's not too much forcing the player to do it and also all that stuff that you can do is not all that complex, just grindy, but I like the grind! It's a cool loop to traverse the galaxy and explore different worlds. I like how you have to interact with a specific race in order to gain reputation and learn their language, again, grindy but actually rewarding because you see the rewards in literally being able to sorta understand the guys after a while. When you actually find the right planet, the right place where the sun shines just right. The game looks great from then on. Even better when you find that moment again, 20 solar systems later. The music is nice I guess, sometimes it fits really nicely but sometimes its a biiiit too much... Base building is cool, resource gathering is cool, I like industrializing hellish planets lol I like the nanite upgrade systems, the feeling of reaching your characters potential movement and damage capacities is nice. Scanner upgrade go BRRRRRRR In general, I would say is a very immersive game, I truly feel like a space traveler when I play No Man's Sky, and I see that as a huge achievement for the game, the movement of the spaceship feels nice most of the time, using the pulse drive and finding stuff in deep space is just cool man. THE BAD: THERES SO MANY BUGS MAN Multiplayer can easily become a very frustrating experience with the bugs, infinite enemy waves, immortal bosses, canceled drops... It happens often, which encourages players/friends to play apart from one another, even more so in combats, which SHOULD be very fun as a team. Speaking about combat... All ground fights are a joke. The only way to make a ground battle remotely challenging is to fight in an infernal world, surrounded by mountains, in the middle of a storm. And still, fighting is just kinda transactional. Spaceship battles are a bit better I think, but not by much: always have sodium/shield rechargers and thats it. I like the mission system in theory, but in practice it feels very shallow and it gets old quick. I understand the way to do it is grab a mission and clear it WHILE you are doing something else/adjacent to it, but still... I just would like something a bit richer from the guild/race missions, not all of them, just maybe from high level missions or something... Thoughts: Go in thinking "Minecraft in space" and you will have a good time! Do not go in thinking "Mass Effect", you will be disappointed.

10 years on, and the game still suffers from problems that seem insignificant at first but end up affecting gameplay if you are in it for more than just the visuals. At some point, when you've made enough discoveries, the oldest ones, be it systems, fauna, flora or minerals will disappear - this includes anything you have added to your wonders list or favourites. Having played this game on PS4, PS5 and now PC, the issues I've found in this game don't seem to be related to the memory limitations of the consoles, but rather the way the game is made. Rendering can sometimes take a long time or just happen at random, sometimes causing you to fall through the terrain or be unable to interact with items or NPC, as an example. Sometimes the visuals can be disorienting, like a bubbling atmosphere or bright colours obscuring your view while in space or on the map trying to make your way to another star system. Also, having more statistics would be an improvement so players could see what actually changes when they purchase and install upgrades. I've put in more than 3000 hours on this game on multiple saves and game modes and the conclusion seems to be that this game is still a work in progress, and while I haven't mentioned every issue I've have to play though in this game, I can say it is still enjoyable and is a great game for those that like sandbox exploration and base building (even though that as well has its limits). Although the "recipe" for planets repeats quite often, the staggering number of star systems still makes it worthwhile exploring and for me personally, trying to find other players' discoveries.

My main save has around 430 hours on it and I've got around 600 total hours in the game. (I migrated it off Xbox and onto Steam) I've watched Hello Games grind out one update after another throughout the years. I will say, this game is absolutely worth the money. At this time there's probably hundreds of hours in quests, content and game systems to explore. So, what does NMS do well? Space! You see a planet and travel seamlessly to it in your chosen spaceship, no load screens, no predetermined place to land. You can drop down and do a flyover and land wherever you like. You can travel to different types of systems, yellow, red, green, blue and purple and explore tons of different kinds of planets. Beautiful and varied- Wow, this game gives me some beautiful screenshots. Some worlds are so beautiful and I find myself just staring at an amazing purple sky at sunset because it's just so damn pretty. Seriously. From the water and the violent waves that occur during storms, to the peaceful sunsets on, this game is so pretty. Spaceships! No matter your style you will find a ship you love, and if you don't, you can make one. From scratch. With living quarters and everything. You can color them, sell them, collect them or strip them down for parts. There are ships everywhere and in every type from massive freighters that have their own quest systems that you can build out into a flying fortresses all the way down to tiny tic-tacs, you like spaceships, you'll find what you want in this game. Variety! This is the core of NMS. Variety in planets, ships, gear, upgrades. Since it's all procedural it's super easy to build out exactly what you want, given you don't mind grinding for it. So many different types of guns, upgrades, ship upgrades, you name it. Things to do! You can explore the cosmos. So many planets, so little time! Build a base, or 2, or 10. You can do quests. Collect and fight space pokemon, Collect dinosaur bones and reassemble them at your base, collect rare ships. Make money, run settlements and grow them into money making endeavors. You can fish, cook, trade, build, explore, use exocraft, recycle, clean up planets, my goodness there's a bunch of things you can do. For all the good, there are some things I'd love to see that I believe would help the game. Fleshed out NPC's- NPC's are copy/paste. You speak to them only to get a word to learn and that's about it. The written lore is fleshed out, both deep and rich but Hello Games didn't follow through with individual NPC's. It's a shame because they gave them such a cool backstory but didn't put it into practice with the actual NPC's. They broke the golden rule of show not tell. There are hundreds of pages of readable lore, but its nebulous and unconnected to any of the inhabitants of the world. Same theme for animals on planets. The creatures are varied and the procedural elements have gotten much better with time. Even after hundreds of hours, I still find creatures that surprise me. The bio features cool flavor text in their bio's but its unrelated to the actual animal. They provide the text, but it's unrelated to the actual animal. With no logical ecosystems, the animals feel soulless and they just kind of mill around a given area. Integrating the cool backstory with the actual creature would really help. Again, show, not tell. POI's - There are limited official Points of Interest. We need more. Dozens more, hundreds more, It's a limitless galaxy but there's only a handful of POI's from world to world. Give me homesteads with different families doing different things. Once again, NMS would do well to show not tell. How about a POI with spawning pools? Or a POI featuring a family of Vykeen with a kid running around? Or different types of ruins? The lore is rich, but in practice every crashed freighter is exactly the same. Make the main quest accessible- I LOVE the Atlas questline. The story is actually phenomenal, but nobody actually knows it because NMS has hidden it behind pages of lore and a language barrier. It's a damn shame that such a cool questline is buried under hard to access lore. Overall this game is amazing, I love it. I'm two thumbs up for what Hello games has accomplished here. They've created a world worth exploring and building in but if they change a few things, they will have created a world I can believe in. I really hope that we see an evolution in these areas with Light No Fire.

I bought No Man's Sky years ago. Back then, recommending it to a friend felt a little like introducing someone to your cousin who had "a rough start in life." You'd immediately start explaining things before they even asked. "Look, I know what happened at launch, BUT..." Today? Today I recommend No Man's Sky with the confidence of a man trying to recruit people into a cult. "Do you have five minutes to talk about our lord and savior, free content updates?" Because somehow this game refuses to stop growing. Every few months I see another update announcement and my first reaction is always: "Wait... they're STILL adding stuff?" At this point I'm convinced the developers accidentally discovered immortality. Most games release. Then they release DLC. Then they release a Definitive Edition. Then they disappear. No Man's Sky releases a major update and immediately starts working on the next one like it owes money to someone. Meanwhile, I'm over here trying to keep up. I originally bought a space exploration game. Now I have: * Built bases. * Built bigger bases. * Built bases I definitely didn't need. * Collected ships. * Collected better ships. * Collected ships because they looked cool. * Become a space explorer. * A space pirate. * A space trader. * A space photographer. * A space archaeologist. * A space hoarder. I have visited planets covered in glowing mushrooms. Planets covered in giant worms. Planets trying very hard to kill me. And planets so beautiful I completely forgot what I was supposed to be doing. The universe is absolutely ridiculous. You land somewhere thinking: "I'll be here for five minutes." Three hours later you're naming alien animals and redesigning a staircase in your base. Again. The visuals are incredible. Every now and then you find a planet that looks so good you stop moving entirely and just stare at it. Then you take screenshots. Then more screenshots. Then even more screenshots. Then you realize you're basically playing Space Tourism Simulator. And somehow after all these years, Hello Games keeps showing up with another free update like: "Hey everyone, we added more stuff." MORE? THERE WAS ALREADY TOO MUCH STUFF. The greatest achievement of No Man's Sky isn't that it became a good game. It's that it became the greatest comeback story in gaming. The launch is one of the most famous disappointments in gaming history. The recovery is one of the most impressive things I've ever seen a developer do. When I first bought the game, I bounced off within hours, didn't even get past the first planet. I was confused, overwhelmed, and hated the pressure of starting in a hazardous planet. It took me a while to reflect, come back, and take the time to give the game a fair shake. And to be fair, I don't see how they could do to improve the tutorial experience at this point. What the new players needs is to take it slow, and take their time to take it all in. Now, I do acknowledge this game still has a ton of issues. I've experiences dozens of bugs myself, nothing game breaking but some immersion breaking. Also, several core systems such as combat are mid at best. The game has a lot of flaws, some things gets repetitive fast, and I would have liked to see more variety when it comes to the planets and their content. Also, from what I've experienced so far, the game is just too easy most of the time, even in survival, or unfairly punitive at other times (like having aggressive creatures spawn in my base, or toxic tornados literally honing on me even inside my base...). Still, by playing this game I felt a soul that I havn't really felt anywhere else... And I trust the devs to keep on improving it. No Man's Sky will soon be 10y old, and there's still a bright future in sight for it. Now I am addicted, and I feel like I've barely scratched the surface still!

Actually, it doesn't suck, it's beyond suckage, it's a drug-addled fever dream on the shoulders of hubris in a trench coat disguised as flight controls. Shame on you. O game não compensa para alguns tipos de pessoas. O game em si até é legal, mas cai no mesmo problema e dilema dos jogos complexos: escolher entre ter muitas mecânicas ou ter poucas, porém boas. O jogo não foca em quase nada. A exploração é realmente legal, mas acaba sendo cansativa para o público que não quer isso. Eu sou do público que veio de jogos de automação industrial (Factorio e Dyson Sphere Program). No início eu não sabia quase nada além do que foi mostrado em 2016. Fiquei ansioso para automatizar, mas depois de horas e horas jogando, descobri que a automação se resume a apenas 4 máquinas muito simples. Isso me fez ficar semanas e meses longe do jogo, pois não faz sentido um título tão simplista. Por exemplo, a mecânica de mineração espacial é muito básica: apenas atirar, atirar e atirar. Deveria evoluir. Adicionar novos scans, novas maneiras de minerar (como laser ou precisar chegar perto, algo como o anime Mighty Space Miners). Mas não. É só atirar e atirar. Esse é o maior problema para pessoas como eu! Eu não quero ficar preso no básico de um jogo. Queria algo mais foda e avançado. A proposta era ambiciosa para uma equipe tão pequena, e no final o que entregaram ficou horrível. Mesmo após todo o caos criado pela Sony, para ser honesto: o game é lixo. Ele é literalmente “explore o genérico”. É como baixar um modpack de Minecraft: sempre a mesma coisa com pequenos detalhes mudados. Para certos tipos de pessoa agrada bastante, mas para mim é horrível, chato pra caralho. Minha impressão final: Game procedural genérico, sem saber o que realmente quer ser. Aeronaves são caras e limitadas, custando de 1 a 10 milhões. Corvettes são extremamente limitadas, com poucos slots e custando 40 milhões(para aumenta os slot e melhorar ela). Fragatas são caras e quase não servem para nada. Automação se resume a um pequeno coletor de oxigênio e um minerador básico. NPCs são genéricos (até mods de Minecraft conseguem ser melhores). Mineração espacial é simplista e horrível: apenas atire no que está na frente... ops, apareceu alguém do seu lado. Cheio de bugs. O problema do game é que ele não sabe o que focar. Portanto, o gameplay é lixo: genérico do genérico, não tem nada de novo. Dicas de melhoria: Aumentar a quantidade de NPCs nos planetas (não apenas nas estações). Tirar eles das bases e dar novas propostas, como NPCs andando pelo planeta com mais personalidade, além de quests (que aliás são uma bosta, pois tudo é ficar indo e voltando pro mesmo lugar). Adicionar mineração mais interessante. Adicionar mais automação. Adicionar mais variedade de aeronaves. Criar uma proposta nova e interessante para corvettes. Na prática, o game é um lixo. Hipoteticamente, eu não compraria novamente de jeito nenhum, porque é simplista. Eu posso instalar mods e fazer um modpack no Minecraft e ter praticamente a mesma experiência que este jogo. Fora que No Man’s Sky praticamente não tem mods, o que fode com tudo. No final, o game não tem quase nada de bom. PT ----------------------------------- English This game is simply not worth it for certain types of players. The game itself isn't terrible, but it suffers from a common problem found in many ambitious games: trying to have a lot of mechanics instead of focusing on a few well-developed ones. No Man's Sky doesn't really excel at anything. Exploration is its strongest aspect, but even that becomes repetitive if you're not the type of player who enjoys endless exploration for its own sake. I come from factory and automation games like Factorio and Dyson Sphere Program. When I started playing, I knew very little about the game besides what was shown back in 2016. I was excited about eventually building large automated systems. After dozens of hours, I discovered that automation basically consists of a handful of very simple machines. That realization made me stop playing for weeks. The mining gameplay is another example. Space mining never evolves. You just keep shooting asteroids forever. There are no advanced mining systems, no specialized equipment, no interesting progression. The game could have introduced scanning mechanics, mining lasers, close-range extraction, mining vessels, or deeper resource systems. Instead, it's just point and shoot from beginning to end. That's the biggest issue for players like me. I don't want to spend hundreds of hours doing the exact same thing with slightly different scenery. I want mechanics that evolve and become more complex over time. The game's ambition was impressive, especially considering the size of the development team. However, the final result feels extremely shallow. Even after all the updates, I still think the core gameplay is fundamentally weak. The entire experience can be summarized as "explore procedural content forever." It's similar to installing a giant Minecraft modpack where everything is technically different, yet somehow feels exactly the same after enough time. My overall impressions: * Generic procedural gameplay that doesn't know what it wants to be. * Ships are expensive and heavily limited. * Freighters are extremely expensive to upgrade and have surprisingly little depth. * Frigates cost a lot and serve very little purpose. * Automation is almost nonexistent. * NPCs are generic and lack personality. * Space mining is painfully simplistic: just shoot whatever is in front of you. * Missions are repetitive fetch quests. * The game is still full of bugs. The biggest problem is that No Man's Sky tries to do everything but doesn't go deep enough into any of its systems. As a result, the gameplay feels generic and repetitive. Things that could improve the game: * More NPCs on planets instead of keeping them mostly in stations and settlements. * NPCs with routines, personalities, and meaningful quests. * More advanced mining mechanics. * Deeper automation and industrial systems. * Greater ship variety and specialization. * More meaningful gameplay for freighters and frigates. * Better mission design instead of endless back-and-forth objectives. Personally, I would never buy this game again. If I want procedural exploration, automation, industry, better NPCs, and deeper progression, I can get most of that from a good Minecraft modpack. For some players, No Man's Sky is an amazing game. For me, it's a shallow experience built around endlessly exploring slightly different versions of the same content.

[h1]Overview[/h1] No Man’s Sky is a vast space‑exploration game where you can roam countless planets, build bases, gather resources, fight, tame and adopt creatures, and hop between vehicles and starships as you travel across the galaxy. There are storylines and questlines to follow as well, giving you direction when you want it. What’s not to like? For survival‑focused players, it’s incredibly easy to fall in love with this universe. With 115 hours in, I want to love it long‑term — but a few things keep pulling me out of the experience. [h1]Review Details[/h1] For anyone interested, here’s a deeper look at my gameplay experience. [h2]The Likes[/h2] [olist] [*] Practically limitless exploration across planets, systems, and galaxies. [*] Discovering new planets, claiming them, renaming them, and earning rewards for scanning flora, fauna, and minerals never gets old. [*] A solid variety of building materials without overwhelming players with unnecessary micro‑details. [*] [spoiler]I absolutely love the exo‑buggy (as I call it) — it’s equipped with the same tools as your multi‑tool, and it’s just fun to use.[/spoiler] [*] Even though I’m not usually a fan of multiple currencies, NMS offers several ways to earn them that aren’t overly demanding. It’s more about finding the method that fits your playstyle and patience. [/olist] [h2]The Dislikes[/h2] [olist] [*] The learning curve for questing can be steep. Even with markers, objectives can be confusing or hard to follow. [*] [spoiler]The galaxy map is confusing, clunky, and takes a while to truly understand.[/spoiler] [*] The save system is frustrating early on. [spoiler]Without a specific upgrade, you can’t manually place a save point, and autosaves can be unpredictable. It’s possible to go 30+ minutes without a save — and if you stop playing, you risk losing everything you just did.[/spoiler] [*] [spoiler]The new Swarm update forced a fresh character. Losing 60 hours on my original save was rough, and when the event ends, I’m stuck choosing between returning to my old character (and leaving rewards behind) or redoing all the quests and upgrades again.[/spoiler] [/olist] [h2]The Wishes[/h2] I know some of these ideas may already be on the devs’ radar, but here are a few things I’d love to see in the future: [olist] [*] Improved questline flow and clearer navigation markers to help new players learn the game more smoothly. [*] A way to map out discovered planets for easier navigation, especially when HUB markers are limited or unclear. [*] NPC companions for gathering, navigation, or even morale — they’d add a lot of personality and utility. [/olist] [h2]The Finds[/h2] A few oddities I ran into during my playthrough: [olist] [*] When hosting, friends sometimes can’t enter my buildings, don’t appear on my screen, or lag behind when loading newly placed objects. [*] [spoiler]I’ve built bases, uploaded them to the galaxy, and returned later only to find another player’s base merged with mine on busy planets — especially Swarm planets.[/spoiler] [/olist] [hr][/hr] [b]Note To Developers:[/b] Wishing you continued success as you grow this game into something even more incredible. I’m rooting for you — and excited to see where No Man’s Sky goes next.

Played on: PS4, PC, XBOX Series X, Steam Deck, and MacOS Played for: overall, I think I probably wasted over 3000 hours on this... Normally, I write the good, the bad, and the ugly, but with this game I need to just describe my feelings. I wanted to love this game, truly, and there were moments where it was fun. But it's not, it gives you a false sense of being far better than it was on release, and a false sense of SO MANY THINGS TO DO, SO MANY PLACES TO GO. But it's all very shallow. Every mechanic they introduce is shallower than a puddle on a sidewalk. Fighting on foot? Garbage. Dogfighting? Garbage. Exploration? Nonexistent, unless you call walking around planets and scanning flora and fauna (and rocks!) as "exploration". The expeditions and events? Laughable and repetitive. Trading? Well, you can buy and sell icons at terminals, and look at your map to see where the best selling price is, fly there, and then sell the icon to the terminal, or a trader who appears once in a blue moon... GREAT... This game is mostly grinding and survival. But when you get the better equipment, the even the survival bit gets repetitive and annoying more than anything, because you're not fighting not to die anymore, you're fighting to not waste time collecting resources. Back in 2016, even in its unfinished state, the game felt like it was trying to show a deep story with existential elements, and to be an unforgettable journey. Now, it feels like a free-to-play survival game from the Let'splayers era on YouTube. And while it's not free-to-play, and we get ALL the new features for FREE, it does cost money, and there are time walls, and various currencies, just like in a F-T-P game. Also, the bugs. Oh lord, there are bugs up the a** in this game. Some are even carried over from the very first 1.0 version, which I did play at launch! Every new update fixes some stuff, while it breaks the rest. There's always some annoying bug that's going to ruin your gameplay, and make you wanna quit. No wonder. This game has been updated and patched, and completely re-written since 2016... The problem isn't the lack of passion from the devs or anything like that. The problem lies in the game engine itself. While it is impressive what they managed to achieve here throughout the years, it's all a shallow and time-wasty experience, due to the fact that they try to appease the fans a little too much... giving them almost everything they want, even if it makes absolutely no sense, and makes the game loose its identity. The game is at its best, when you've never played it, and it's your first time experience, discovering the storyline, all the gameplay mechanics, activities, and getting bombarded with "possibilities". Or if you're a veteran and you play the permadeath mode. THAT is interesting and challenging. So yeah, I'm really sorry I got duped into thinking that "this next update will surely make the game better, right?". No, unless the devs come up with a way to REALLY make the game grow, instead of adding countless useless features to it (we have Pokemon battles in it, for ****s sake!).

One of the first things people ask me is, "is this game glitchy?" If you're one of those retentive wackadoos that can't handle a little chop when a mass amount of assets are loading and start throwing your controller every time the game skips a few frames, turn around and walk the other way while the rest of us enjoy what this UNIVERSE has to offer. Still reading? Good. If you like a game with replayability, this is one of those. This game caters to people that want to do a lot in their game. I've been playing since Beta, and it's come a long, long way. The cross-save is really smooth (couldn't access the newest features from a certain money-grabbing "leading" console company) Ship combinations were pretty extensive, and then they started letting you put together ships from your favorite parts. And THEN they gave us Corvettes, fully customizable ships that you can stop and walk around in, and even bring your friends along for the ride. You can mine and craft. You can base-build to your heart's content on multiple worlds. Cook. Fish. Hunt. Brawl. Race. But my favorite part, Travelers... is the exploration. I've come across worlds that give you infinite screenshot options (and that interface has a lot to offer in itself), character customization, regular Expeditions (limited events with loot for customizing characters, ships, etc). You can explore solo, battle your companion creatures three-on-three against other Travelers, or just wander. I think the worst time I'm having with this game is this. Right here. Writing a review is near impossible because there is so much I could rave on and on about. So if you want to get into something that's going to keep you busy and is VERY easy to pick back up after a long time away, this is the one. No Man's Sky. It's not about the planet. It's not about the races of the characters. It's not about the history or the future. It's about everything.

It turns out that you just have to let the countless--uninvited--NPCs on your ship fly it and do stuff on it without you ever being able to. You can land your tiny "starships" inside this big ship and put your items in its storage, but that's about it. Okay, now that I've yapped on about what I don't like, I want to clarify that this is a great game and that you should still play it. The story is deep. The sense of discovery is surreal. The infinite universe is overwhelming. Its truly fascinating. You can travel to distant stars and visit countless planets, each unique from the last. The base building is great. You obtain tools to manipulate terrain and discover recipes to build structures and items. Overall, this game is very good, but the system for the ships you fly in could be better.

As someone who absolutely adores sci-fi, astronomy, space exploration, and games like Mass Effect... *cue the Hans Zimmer playlist* No Man's Sky scratches an itch that very few games ever have.. There's something genuinely magical about landing on a planet you've never seen before, stepping out of your ship, glancing up at a sky that quite literally exists nowhere else, and having absolutely no clue what you're about to stumble into. Sometimes it's a paradise world with glowing grass, colossal rings stretching across the heavens, floating islands, and colours so absurdly gorgeous I'm half convinced my graphics card is just showing off. Other times... it's an inhospitable frozen wasteland where I'm fighting for my life every thirty seconds, or a toxic planet that essentially greets me with, "Welcome! Now perish." Bit rude, if you ask me. There's also something this game makes me feel that I don't think I've experienced anywhere else. An existential crisis. No, genuinely. Every now and then I'll land on some random planet in some random galaxy that I'll almost certainly never visit again. I'll stop, look up at the stars, realize how laughably microscopic I am in the grand scheme of the universe, and suddenly I'm questioning the meaning of my existence instead of collecting Carbon. Mate... I logged in to scan rocks. Why am I suddenly having a philosophical debate with myself? Half the time I'll completely forget whatever objective I was supposed to be doing because I'm busy watching freighters silently drift across the void, standing there as planets slowly rise over the horizon, following ships weaving through the atmosphere, or wandering around ancient alien ruins for an embarrassingly long amount of time. The universe has this uncanny way of making me stop and simply... exist in it for a while. While the game certainly isn't perfect, it's improved so dramatically over the years that it's honestly rather astonishing. If I had one wish, it'd be for the multiplayer experience to feel a touch more polished and interactive, and for the NPCs to have a bit more personality. That's probably just the Mass Effect fan in me talking. I'm far too accustomed to unforgettable companions, brilliant conversations, and characters who make the galaxy feel inhabited. Every now and then I wish the people in No Man's Sky felt just a little more... alive. Even so, it never really diminishes what the game does best. Because there's always another star system waiting to be explored. Another peculiar little alien creature waiting to be discovered. Another breathtaking planet. Another impossibly beautiful ship hiding somewhere out in the darkness. For a game about exploring an infinite universe, I don't think I've ever grown tired of looking up.

So, I have astrophobia (and yes, I did buy a $60 game based on my fear), and after playing around with the game, it has actually helped over the 10 hours I've played it. While I still prefer to play with friends, I feel much more comfortable playing alone now, even if I have to use super loud music. As a side note, my astrophobia isn't major at all, but it becomes much worse when I'm actually playing a game about it. I love watching videos of people playing space games like NMS; however, whenever I try to play one myself, I usually get scared. But besides my personal issues, this game is beautiful, and I know that anybody interested in space and has the money to buy it would absolutely love it. It's one of those games where there's almost too much to do, and you get slightly overwhelmed when you realize there's a full story to complete. Most of the planets are quite diverse, at least from the 15 or so planets I've seen (which isn't really a lot at all). My only complaint is that there are very few ways to die, and even then, death isn't much of a problem unless you're playing on Permadeath mode. The only time I've died was when my friend shot me to death </3. Overall, this is one of the best-designed games I've ever played. With over 18 quintillion planets and countless things to do, there's always something new to discover.

I was interested in this game for a long while because of all the praise it's gotten for being the game that had a terrible launch but was worked on so much by the developers afterwards. However, I can't give this game that same praise. I started No Man's Sky with high hopes, excited to explore space and build stuff. Instead, the game started with a confusing tutorial that wouldn't tell me where to find a specific material, only to later tell me the objective was about 1km away. So I walked. And walked. And walked until I finally got to my ship, only to find out it needed repairs. The closest repair part was ALSO about 1km away, so I spent over 5 minutes walking there and another 5 minutes walking back. I repair the ship and... it's still not done. After locating more materials and refining them, I was finally able to fly away from the planet. Only to find out my next objective was on the same planet, meaning I had to go right back. At this point, the game had been 1% fun and 99% walking. Then it tells me to find a specific mineral deposit. I searched around for 15 minutes before it finally appeared within scanner range, and then I had to walk back to my ship again. After finally unlocking build mode and trying it out, I'd had enough. No Man's Sky may become interesting later on, but the early game is such a slog. It's just walking, walking, and more walking, with no interesting story to keep me invested. It doesn't matter how good a game gets 10, 20, or 50 hours in if it can't keep me entertained during the first hour.

With a very heavy heart I have to leave a negative review for this game. The game showed so much potential, it definitely has a SOUL, and the creators have a really good eye for details, and it is not a bad game by any means. However, so many core mechanics are flawed that it makes me cry in real life. I really looked forward to playing this game together with my husband, but that experience turned into a catastrophic failure. Base Building: You cannot build a base together because the base computer is personalized. You can't even place them side by side. Terrain in multiplayer bugs horribly. What you remove using the terraforming tool comes back; what you add disappears. Buildings sink, and NPCs clip through the floor. Spaceships & Capital Ships: You cannot build your spaceship together. You can't even invite your friend to your capital ship, as they get placed into a completely different instance. You cannot even properly see your friend's ship name. The "Co-op" Corvette: The only spaceship designed to fly together (the corvette) does not work properly in multiplayer. The mission board does not properly sync between you and your friend, you can get teleported out of the ship if you stand in the wrong spot, and you are not allowed to add parts to help your friend build it. Many other minor glitches on top of those. Broken Quests: Many quests are impossible to complete if you are in someone else's game. NPCs who talked to your friend will no longer talk to you, and destination markers bug out and lead to nowhere. This game is absolutely not for completionists or people who love collecting in-game items: FOMO / Past Content: Most of the coolest stuff you encounter or have seen in trailers (including spaceships) you will never ever get. They come from past expeditions that are over, and today there is no way to complete them. Your collection inventory is strictly limited. You have N amount of spaceships you can own and save, N amount of weapons, an N amount of pets, and only 10 storage chests. The quest designer should be fired. These are the worst, most boring (bordering on annoying) quests I have ever seen in any game, with a complete joke instead of actual rewards. It is just endless moving from point A to point B without any meaningful gameplay. On top of it the quest log is a calamity. Most of the dialogues are just an illusion of choice — different options either lead to the exact same outcome or force you to go through all of them regardless. The only dialogue where "choice matters" locks you out of important game mechanic. Boring Combat: Both space and land enemies pose a threat only in the very beginning. Later on, you can just completely ignore their presence. Pointless Economy: So much effort was put into different economy mechanics, yet none of them are actually needed. Currency is a problem only in the first few hours; after that, you get more money than you can ever spend just by passively scanning flora and fauna along the way. So many other mechanics serve no real purpose other than ticking a checkbox: "we have fishing in our game", "we have cooking in our game". You will never actually need to use them.

[h2]No Man’s Sky is a silver-threaded dream across the stars.[/h2] [i]After 57 hours, this has become one of my favorite games I have played in a long time — and easily one of the best space games I have ever experienced.[/i] [hr][/hr] No Man’s Sky is more than a game about flying ships, gathering resources, upgrading gear, or discovering planets. At its best, it is a game about wonder. It captures that rare feeling of stepping onto an unknown world, looking up at an alien sky, and realizing there is still something beautiful waiting beyond the next star. There is a quiet magic here that feels personal. The universe is massive, but it never feels meaningless. It feels lonely in a peaceful way, beautiful in a strange way, and comforting in a way I did not expect. One moment you are breaking through a planet’s atmosphere, and the next you are standing beneath strange moons, watching unfamiliar creatures move across a world that feels like it was waiting for you to find it. [b]That is where No Man’s Sky shines brightest:[/b] it gives you freedom without taking away the sense of mystery. [list] [*][b]Explore[/b] endless planets, systems, creatures, and landscapes. [*][b]Build[/b] bases that feel like little homes beneath unfamiliar skies. [*][b]Upgrade[/b] ships, tools, freighters, and technology at your own pace. [*][b]Drift[/b] through space with no pressure, following whatever signal catches your heart. [/list] What I love most is that the game lets you create your own rhythm. Some sessions are about progression. Some are about survival. Some are about building, trading, fighting, or collecting. And sometimes, the best moments are the quiet ones: landing on a beautiful planet, listening to the wind, watching the stars, and simply existing in the universe. The atmosphere is incredible. The visuals feel like classic science fiction art brought to life — colorful skies, glowing landscapes, strange wildlife, storm-wrapped planets, and ships cutting through space like silver comets. The music and sound design add so much emotion, from the hum of your ship to the silence of deep space. No Man’s Sky is not perfect. Some parts can feel repetitive or grindy, and players who need constant action may not connect with its slower pace. But for me, that slower pace is part of the beauty. Mining, scanning, flying, warping, and discovering become almost meditative — a silver tide of quiet exploration. After 57 hours, I still feel like I have only scratched the surface. There are still planets to find, ships to collect, bases to build, and stars to chase. This game hit my heart in a way I did not expect. [b]Peaceful. Massive. Strange. Beautiful. Unforgettable.[/b] [h3]A silver tide of stars, wonder, and discovery. Highly recommended.[/h3]

I've been playing No Man's Sky since day one, and I can honestly say I've never seen a game transform the way this one has. What started as an ambitious space exploration game has become one of the greatest redemption stories in gaming history. Over the years, Hello Games has continued to deliver massive free updates that have expanded nearly every aspect of the experience: exploration, base building, freighters, settlements, expeditions, multiplayer, ship customization, planetary variety, and so much more. The sense of scale remains incredible. Even after all these years, I still find myself landing on a new planet and discovering something I've never seen before. Whether I'm exploring distant star systems, building a new base, hunting for rare ships, or simply enjoying a sunset on an alien world, the game constantly reminds me why I keep coming back. What impresses me most is the passion and dedication of the developers. Instead of abandoning the project, they kept improving it year after year, turning it into something truly special. Few studios have shown this level of commitment to their community. No Man's Sky isn't just a good game anymore—it's a remarkable journey that continues to evolve. If you've ever dreamed of exploring an endless universe at your own pace, this is one of the best experiences available. After playing since launch, I can confidently recommend it. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

It also has time travel of sorts, from what I understand. For such a simple system, this game is absolutely massive, and I will absolutely recommend it. I have to fully recommend this game. The game allows you to put in as much or as little time as possible. You can waste time exploring the galaxy(ies), and completely ignore the missions if that's what you want to do. There's no penalty for ignoring things. The learning curve is smooth, and leads directly into the next stage which is always explained through the tutorial missions. The combat is satisfying, and the escalation of sentinel encounters really does give you a sense of urgency if you aren't prepared to deal with them. Finding derelict ships to sell is one of my favorite activities, and how i also found my favorite fighter. You can also build a corvette in pretty much any style you want with the prefab mods, if ugly or beauty is your thing it's not difficult to do either. The ability to have a mobile space station that can hold all of your ships and stuff is something else as well. Especially when you can just walk out into outer space and just look around. The graphics are engaging, the sound quality is great, the music fits the mood of the differing scenes, and the seamless transition from planet to space to space station just feels great. Overall, solid 9/10.

I played no man's sky on release day on ps4. I played it for longer than most people should. I loved my time with it... i'm a big ol sci fi fan so its not hard for a space game to grab my attention. I'm going to recommend this game to people that haven't played it like me, cause you don't know. Now here is my critique... The first SEVERAL hours of this game are LITERALLY unchanged from its initial release. Nothing feels different, you are mining grabbing stuff, and just spend your first few hours doing the same things you did ON DAY 1 with a few extra steps and things you need to upgrade. Which for me? was extremely off putting... Then I got into the settlement stuff, started having fun with that, and then you have to wait 20/40/50/2 hours to complete a building. I'm sure the intent is for you to do things in the mean time, but I don't like it. Why can't i upgrade multiple buildings? its not like it takes citizens to upgrade them? if it did i would prioritize getting citizens but it doesn't... So why can't i upgrade multiple things at once? this is the part where i realized this game is okay with wasting your time. I jumped on to upgrade a building that would take 2 hours to finish upgrading. I then went to work out, and make food, and came back to realize what i had always feared but i had just forgotten to do. If you don't jump into your ship and jump out to save that EXTREMELY important interaction/upgrade. Guess what? it never happened. I'm at the point in time in my life where I dont like games that waste my time, or have mechanics where i have to wait, especially if it doesn't make sense. why can't i upgrade my overseer building and the more i upgrade that the more upgrades i can have active at a single time? why can't i see the materials i need so i can go gather them while its upgrading? it just says "you have an active upgrade happening on another building" come on bro... that's just cheeks. maybe its totally my fault and I should haven't messed with settlements so early? then maybe i shouldn't be allowed to interact with one until i've done certain milestones, but then that sucks too. I don't know. Maybe i'm just crazy and nobody else feels this way, which is possible. Once again though, i have been enjoying the game, but i do feel like there are elements of this game that just want to waste my time, and i'm not about that, and i don't know if i will continue to play more of this because of that. i'm gonna thumb this up cause i think my problem just may be a ME thing, and not something everyone else will have, and others may enjoy it. there also isn't a neutral recommendation, if there is i am dumb and don't see it LMAO

No Man's Sky has a history. The game launched in a rough place, and folks accused the devs of false advertisement of their game, without acknowledging their release deadline was forced upon them, and that they lost almost half of what they had even made for the game to flooding in the studio not long before said release. The game still definitely launched in a rough state, few people will deny that, but the game today is a much better product. Disclaimer: Everything in this game is procedurally generated. That means you will see some repeated body parts on animals, shapes in rocks and plants, and general terrain similarities between planets. This is more like Minecraft in that sense; things can only be so different from one world to the next unless we want to give up and AI generate all the assets for every planet. But the amount of variety will rarely have things looking too samey, and the game looks pretty phenomenal on most settings, you might need a decently powerful PC to run it though. You will be simulating a small, simplified solar system in real time, outside of the nearby surface of the planet you are currently on. You won't find many games that do have the functioning ability to hop into your space ship, take off, ascend to space, and then land on another planet seamlessly, though. Not even the far newer Starfield with a far larger dev team and budget can make that claim. The bulk of this game is trading, collecting, and exploring. You will upgrade your suit, your mining tool, your base and its components, and eventually entire space freighters and squads of ships. There are even big community raid events that come out every so often. And most of this tech being incorporated into this game today will be used in their next game, Light No Fire, a single-planet fantasy-themed alternative with a lot of similar bones. Which I am very excited for. This game is not super brutally realistic. It is fairly mechanically simple, all things considered. But there's plenty to see, and if you're looking for a chill space game that will let you build cool ships and bases on alien worlds with your friends, this is it. I just wish I had more friends to play it with myself :')

This is honestly one of the best sci-fi and space-themed games I've ever played ( after Elite Dangerous ofc). I literally fell in love with this game. Ever since I was a kid, I've been fascinated by space. I've spent countless hours reading about the universe, learning about planets, stars, black holes, and the possibility of extraterrestrial life. The idea that there could be something beyond our world has always captured my imagination, and that's one of the reasons why No Man's Sky feels so special to me. The sense of exploration in this game is incredible. Landing on completely unknown planets, discovering strange creatures, traveling through vast star systems, and simply looking at the sky from an alien world never gets old. It gives me the feeling of being part of a huge, living universe where there's always something new waiting to be found. What I love most is how the game lets you create your own adventure. Sometimes I spend hours exploring planets, sometimes building bases, and other times just flying through space and enjoying the atmosphere. The freedom it offers is something I rarely find in other games. As someone who has always dreamed about space exploration and the possibility of life beyond Earth, No Man's Sky feels like a game made for people like me. It's not just a game about survival or progression it's a game that lets you experience the wonder of the unknown. For me that's what makes it one of the greatest space games ever made.

Whether you enjoy survival, building, collecting, or simply wandering through beautiful alien worlds, this game offers hundreds of hours of content. No Man's Sky is a great example of how a game can grow into something truly special through dedication and continuous support from its developers. Highly recommended for anyone who loves space, exploration, and adventure.

Subject: Suggestion for future updates: Making fauna more aggressive and dangerous Hi Hello Games team! First of all, thank you for your incredible and dedicated work on No Man's Sky. The game has evolved beautifully, but there is one aspect that many veteran players feel is currently lacking: the danger and unpredictability of fauna. Right now, exploring planets can feel a bit too safe. Most creatures are passive, and even the "aggressive" ones rarely pose a real threat. To make exploration more thrilling and less repetitive, please consider adding or tweaking the following: True Predators: We need creatures that actually hunt the player actively, stalk them from the shadows, or attack in packs. High-Danger Planets: Introduce worlds where the fauna is extremely hostile, requiring players to fully upgrade their multi-tool weapons and shields just to survive a short walk. Apex Predators: Giant, boss-like creatures on specific planets that offer rare rewards upon defeat. Better AI: Make predators smarter—let them camouflage, pounce from trees, or burrow underground to surprise us. Adding a real element of danger to the wildlife would bring back that amazing feeling of steping into the unknown and genuinely fighting for survival. Thank you for listening to the community!

i think it's time to start talking about No Man Sky's goat status Crazy that all these DLC worthy updates are just for free every time. Not only is the game so great it would take probably lifetimes to see and do everything that the game already offers, but it keeps getting greater and more interesting every couple months!.. Red dead redemption in space (why bother making a star wars game now?) mixed in with some subnautica, and, oh the map is infinite by the way, you can build fully customizable spacecrafts, edit and modify the world in minecraft-like ways, manage settlements into profitability, the space combat is REALLY good, the FPS aspect has gotten a lot better (love the PvP), I think the multiplayer is seamlessly integrated into the game, it's really fun and nice to see. I could go on and on, there are so many other features to this game, POKEMON now for god's sake,,, this game really has it all man, and the world is so much richer for it. The only and only tiny tiny note I'd have is, and this is not made to discourage you from getting the game, it's more of an open note, I sometimes wish there were more variety and wonder in the species that exist; I could imagine conscious "clouds", forms of life that much like fungi might spread on a wall they spread among the clouds through ionization of the gases, but it could really just be simple adjustments in how the variability of the characteristic types of the species. Too many species end up looking like different skins of the same other species, which makes sense when you think of evolutionary convergence and adaptability and whatnot, but I think it'd be really interesting if there was a environmental (including notions of atmosphere density/thickness and gravity, among others) attribute randomizer for at least a few aspects of their looks/behaviors, especially the basic shape of their bodies, since in the end none of these life forms should realllly look like they're from the same planet if they're not. Maybe I've started to play it too much, but part of me kinda wants to feel truly surprised at seeing some of those life forms (and there are already plenty in the game that do provoke that experience, I just wish it was a more common experience).

We all know the story of no man's sky at this point. I have real respect to the devs for continuing to put out new updates to this game year after year. Never once have they charged me for a dlc, battle pass, or some kind of cosmetic. Despite all this i dont really know if i can recommend no man's sky. as a teen i had put nearly 200 hours into this game and since then roughly 30 or so more when i come by to see whatever expansion catches my eye. its a game i want to like. its just really, really, really boring. looking at it now i can imagine that the first time you play it this game is really cool. theres lots of things to do, lots of things to see, but as you go around doing and seeing these thing they all start to blend together. youve seen one tropical planet youve seen them all. exploration on the whole is a bust, its the same buildings everywhere with a different coat of paint, the same sentinels, the same repeatable quests. the expeditions serve as a temporary distraction from this sameness, a nice little questline that shows you the in and out of a new update. my only real issue with them is that they are timegated. but even they dont solve the core issue. once you know how to easily get a good weapon, how to easily get currency, how to easily get a good ship then even the expeditions fall apart and your forced to look at what gameplay these tools exist in service of. grounded combat is bad, the camera is far to interested in the back of the players head and first person is quite ugly somehow. the sentinels pose no real threat to the player incredibly quickly, becoming more of a increasingly ignorable annoyance and a occasional good source of nanites. the small dissident sentinels have had a issue where their drops spawn to low to the ground and fall out of bounds for as long as i can remember them in the game. space combat is somehow worse. the game likes to have big showpiece fights in space, the raider dreadnaught for example, but the combat in those fights is holding s + m1. your ship will auto target anything in range, so you dont need to even look at the screen if you dont want to. it actively ruins the upgrade system for me because no matter how much i want to care about number go up tricknology the number will never meaningfully matter. all of this results in what is to me a sad game. a endless ocean with the depth of a puddle. its a shame that so much passion has resulted in such a empty game. i assume its a issue with technical debt, the game has been getting updated for a long while now and hello games were not a experienced dev team at the start. at this point i dont think any amount of updates will "fix" the core of this game. personally id like to see them start fresh and make something new. i think they could do a lot better this time

On the first day I learned how to survive in my exosuit on a hostile planet, repaired a crashed starship, built a simple base, explored other planets in the system, visited the local orbital station, met many aliens, and began learning their languages. On the second day I fixed the starship's warp drive, explored a nearby system and several planets, repaired a crashed starship enough to get it to an orbital and sell it for salvage, and expanded my base to include power generation, a teleporter, and storage. On the third day I explored a half-dozen more star systems while doing missions, salvaged and repaired a crashed starship which became my new primary starship, enhanced my base with solar panels and batteries, saved a freighter fleet from pirates, and in gratitude was given command of the fleet. On the fourth day a second frigate joined my freighter fleet, I sent the frigates on a few expeditions, added storage, a refinery, a teleporter, and trade interface to my freighter, added a starship landing pad and exocraft garage to my base, built a corvette class starship and began working on getting materials to build its interior equipment, and became the overseer of a troubled settlement on a dangerous world. It can be somewhat overwhelming but is an incredible game.

This game is actually one of the most overrated pieces of garbage I’ve ever wasted money and time on. People kept hyping it up like it was some limitless universe exploration masterpiece, but after a few hours you realize the entire game loop is just mining rocks, refilling oxygen, refilling fuel, refilling life support, and staring at procedurally generated planets that all feel the exact same with different color filters slapped on top. “No Man’s Sky” should honestly be renamed to “No Man’s Fun.” Every planet is: * land on planet * scan 3 ugly animals * collect ferrite dust for the 900th time * repair some broken garbage * fly to another empty planet * repeat forever until your brain melts The exploration is fake depth. There are billions of planets but somehow all of them feel soulless. After the first 10 planets you’ve basically seen the entire game already. Wow, another toxic wasteland with weird broccoli-looking creatures walking around. Incredible innovation. And the inventory management is absolutely miserable. Half the gameplay is just cleaning your backpack like you’re working in a cosmic warehouse simulator instead of exploring space. Every five minutes: “Inventory full.” “Technology damaged.” “Not enough fuel.” “Hazard protection falling.” SHUT UP. The combat is terrible, the gunplay feels like shooting plastic toys, space battles are stiff and repetitive, and enemy AI has the intelligence of a dying toaster. Even pirates somehow manage to make space combat feel boring. And don’t even get me started on multiplayer. The universe is supposedly infinite yet somehow everything still feels empty and lifeless. Playing with friends just turns the grind into co-op suffering. “Bro come help me farm carbon for 40 minutes so we can build another ugly metal box base on a planet nobody cares about.” People defend this game because of the updates, but adding 500 updates to a boring core game is like putting glitter on a trash bag. Sure, there’s “more content” now, but most of it is shallow systems stacked on top of other shallow systems. Pets, settlements, freighters, expeditions — all of it sounds cool for about 15 minutes before turning into another repetitive grind loop. The game constantly pretends it’s deep and philosophical too. Every NPC talks like a broken AI generated fortune cookie: “Traveler… the Atlas… the anomaly… existence… kzzzt.” Bro just let me skip the dialogue. And visually? Yeah, it looks pretty sometimes — for screenshots. Actually playing it feels like wandering through an AI-generated wallpaper collection with zero emotional impact. The planets don’t feel handcrafted, memorable, or alive. They feel mathematically assembled. Because they are. Honestly the biggest enemy in No Man’s Sky isn’t pirates, aliens, or survival mechanics. It’s boredom. I’ve had more excitement organizing files on my desktop than exploring another randomly generated radioactive snow planet for the 80th time. The craziest part is that the game somehow manages to make SPACE feel small. SPACE. One of the coolest concepts imaginable. And they turned it into an infinite loading screen full of chores.

Borderline thumbs-up. The game's [b]basic design[/b] hasn't changed since its release. I still find the same shape for multiple kinds of minerals, weirdly-moving procedurally-generated creatures, objects spawning in the air, or enemies far below the ground. There are also many [b]similar mechanics with different graphics[/b] - it doesn't matter if it's a radiation supercell or snow storm, it acts the almost same, and prompts the same behaviour from me. But, 10 years of slow-but-steady updates did smooth out the largest bugs, [b]added content[/b], and implemented requested features. The game is still very, [b]very grindy[/b]. I'm playing with custom difficulty settings to remove inventory busywork (maximum inventory slots, maximum inventory stack size, no limits to inventory transfer range), and it makes it more tolerable. After a busy day at work, when I can barely think, it is relaxing to just mine some minerals, or add a few walls to my base. So, if you enjoy playing a grindy game which doesn't require much thinking, and can deliver some pretty nice images (but still has a bit of jank), No Man's Sky is [b]okay[/b]. I feel the asking price is far too high for the shallow gameplay and the remaining bugs, but I did get it at a very steep [b]discount[/b]. And the studio's long-term efforts to support the game after its disastrous state at launch are laudable. So, yes. After being very against No Man's Sky for a decade, I'll say this: it's OK.

There's a story about a version of hell that is a possibly infinite library, in which the damned must search forever for a book that recounts their entire life story amongst the never-ending volumes, most of which are gibberish. No Man's Sky is that in game form. NMS is not a very good game: the mining, the base building and the combat are bad, bad in that that every interaction is unsatisfying and hollow. Its only dance move is to make you search for things to put in your inventory. There are a lot of things to put in your inventory. Every update has added more. None of these things matter once acquired or feel different from one another, but you'll have a lot of them in your inventory, which will end up split across the cargo hold of various space ships and exocraft. Occasionally you will have to scour the galaxy for very particular things to put in your inventory. A long while back, nearer release, Cool Ghosts described NMS as "a shapes and colours simulator", which is still accurate and absolutely the mindset you must approach this game with in order to enjoy it. You must pootle, prod and generally let the post rock soundtrack and technicolour visuals wash over you. This feeling is great while it lasts, the mood is immaculate when the proc gen throws you a stunning vista or a planet that is fun to navigate. A mood somewhat at odds with the need to constantly shovel resources into various life-support systems, since 95% of planets have inhospitable atmospheres. The story and various bits of finely-tuned writing are homeopathic in their effectiveness (barring the major revelation at the end of the main quest, which is the perfect explanation of why the game is as hollow-feeling as it is). How could it be otherwise? Randomly serving nihilistic vignettes and sad snippets of woe that players might find in a random order in vastly differing contexts is all the foundations of the game can allow for. It adds to the faintly hypnotic aura of the game, since even the most crafted snippet of text has to be as interchangeable as all those inventory items, everything blends together. NMS is not a very good game. But it is a big mood. It's absolutely at odds with itself. It's fascinating.
